item.title: How Will You Measure Your Life (Christensen): strategy, allocation, and the 98 percent rule
item.description: Clayton Christensen's 2012 book as the fourth and final antidote – the ten minutes Andy Grove wouldn't give him, resource allocation as a life's real strategy, Herzberg's noble profession, the Sunday basketball game and the ninety-eight percent rule, jobs-to-be-done applied to a marriage, and the case against: Jill Lepore's assault on the parent theory and a book that never turns its own tools on itself.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Ten Minutes Andy Grove Wouldn't Give Him

Before he published The Innovator's Dilemma, Clayton Christensen got a call from Andrew Grove, then the chairman of Intel. Grove had read an early paper of his on disruptive technology and wanted it explained to his direct reports. Christensen flew to California, excited, and showed up at the appointed hour to hear Grove say: stuff has happened, we have ten minutes, tell us what your model means for Intel. Christensen said he couldn't, that the model needed thirty minutes of setup or nothing about Intel would make sense. Ten minutes into the explanation anyway, Grove cut him off again: I've got your model. Just tell us what it means for Intel.

Christensen held his ground a second time. He asked for ten more minutes to walk the room through a different industry first, steel, where mills like Nucor had started at the cheap end of the market, reinforcing bars for concrete, and worked their way up until they had swallowed the businesses that used to look down on them. When he finished the steel story, Grove said he got it, and started talking, out loud, toward the strategy that would become Intel's decision to build a stripped-down, cut-rate chip aimed at the bottom of the market rather than defending the high end. He named it after himself in the room. Celeron.

Christensen said afterward that he thought about that meeting a million times. If he had told Grove what to think about microprocessors, he'd have been thrown out. Instead he taught him how to think, and Grove reached the answer on his own, and believed it because he had built it. That became Christensen's method for the rest of his career: when a company asked what to do, he ran their question through a model built from someone else's industry, and let them answer it themselves.

Late in his life, on the last day of the class he taught every year at Harvard Business School, Christensen turned that same method on the students in the room, and asked them to point it at themselves. Not at a company. At a career, a marriage, and the question of whether they would end up, twenty years on, somewhere they could still recognize. The book this episode is about is what happened when a man who spent thirty years teaching corporations how to see their own blind spots ran the same instrument over his own life, and then handed it to several million readers who had never sat in his classroom and had no professor in the room to catch what the instrument couldn't see.

Chapter Two: The Man Running Out of Time to Say It

Clayton Christensen was born in Salt Lake City in nineteen fifty-two, the second of eight children, and grew up wanting to run a newspaper before an economics degree at Brigham Young University pointed him toward business. He won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford in nineteen seventy-five, took a doctorate in applied econometrics, and worked at Boston Consulting Group and then at a ceramics start-up he co-founded before landing, in his late thirties, back at Harvard as a doctoral student and then a professor. The book that made him famous, The Innovator's Dilemma, came out in nineteen ninety-seven, and Grove told a reporter that year it was the one book that had taught him more than anything else he had read in a decade. Christensen spent the next two decades refining and re-testing the theory of disruption across hard drives, steel, retailing, and eventually his own field, higher education and health care, while raising five children with Christine, the wife he had met as an undergraduate at Brigham Young University, and building a reputation as the rare management theorist whom chief executives actually returned calls to.

He was also, for most of that time, dying by installments, a fact the book leans on without ever naming it outright. A heart attack opened the pattern in two thousand and seven. Two years later a doctor found a follicular lymphoma. Then, that same spring, mid-sentence at a church meeting, came a stroke that left him unable to find words for sentences he could still think with perfect clarity; he spent months relearning to speak around the gap it left. Harvard's graduating class asked him to address them that very spring, weeks after the stroke, and asked him not to talk about business. They wanted to know what he had learned about living. What became the book started as that speech, delivered by a man who had just watched his own vocabulary go missing and come back changed. A kidney cancer followed, and finally a form of leukaemia that his own doctors traced back to the treatments for the earlier illnesses; he died in January of twenty twenty, at sixty-seven.

None of that appears as a plot point in the book itself; it surfaces once, briefly, in the final pages, and I will come back to it there. But it belongs in the room from the first page, because a theory of how to spend your limited time carries a different weight when the man proposing it has just been told, twice, how limited his own turned out to be.

Chapter Three: The Question Nobody Had Assigned Him

The class Christensen taught was called Building and Sustaining a Successful Enterprise, and for most of the semester it did exactly what the title promised: a backbone of management theory, with a different company examined each session through whichever lens the day's theory supplied. On the last day, he turned the lenses on the students instead, and asked them to find real answers to three questions: how a career keeps its promise of happiness, how a marriage and a family end up an enduring source of it rather than a casualty, and how a person stays out of jail.

He meant the third one literally. Two of the thirty-two Rhodes scholars in his own Oxford class spent time in prison. Jeffrey Skilling, of Enron, had been his classmate at Harvard Business School. Christensen's point to his students was not that criminals are a different species from Harvard graduates; it was that nobody in either cohort had enrolled with a plan to end up there, and something in the ordinary accumulation of small decisions had carried some of them across a line they never meant to approach.

The article that grew out of the speech carried a sidebar the book itself later drops, brief testimonials from that graduating class, gathered months after markets had cratered under people who had planned confidently on climbing straight from business school into finance. One of them, Patrick Chun, on his way to a private equity firm, put the shift in mood better than Christensen's own prose does: students, he said, had stopped asking where the maximum was and started asking, in his words, "what's the minimum I need to have, and what else drives my life?" It is a plainer, more urgent version of the same three questions Christensen was about to put to them himself.

Word of the speech reached Karen Dillon, then the editor of the Harvard Business Review, who asked whether it could be written up as an article. It ran that July under the title this episode borrows, won the magazine's award for the year's best piece, and became, in twenty twelve, a book, co-written with Dillon and a former student named James Allworth, that expanded the same three questions into chapters. The book keeps the classroom structure. Career, family, integrity, in that order, each one answered by importing a piece of management theory that Christensen had spent his research life building for boardrooms, and running it, in front of the reader, over a life instead of a company.

Chapter Four: The Manager Who Drove Home Twice

The first question, how to be sure of happiness in a career, gets answered with a theory that predates the book by decades: Frederick Herzberg's argument, from nineteen fifty-nine, that job satisfaction and job dissatisfaction are not opposite ends of one scale but two separate instruments. Pay, status, job security, and working conditions are what Herzberg called hygiene factors: get them wrong and people are miserable, but getting them right doesn't make anyone happy, it only stops them being unhappy. The things that actually produce satisfaction are a different list entirely: the chance to learn something, to take on responsibility, to be recognised for doing something that mattered. A raise removes a complaint. It does not manufacture the feeling of a life well spent.

Christensen illustrates the theory with an image he says came to him while he still ran his own company, before the professorship: a manager of his leaving for work one morning with a decent level of self-regard, and then, in his mind, driving home ten hours later feeling small, unused, and unseen, and he pictured what that does to the way she talks to her own children that evening. Then he ran the identical shift forward a second way, ending instead with her walking in the door full rather than empty, having built something and been told it mattered. His conclusion, delivered in the flattest possible terms for a claim this large, was that management, done well, is the most noble of the professions, because no other work hands one person so many daily chances to help someone else grow, take responsibility, and be recognised for it.

It is worth sitting for a moment with how strange that sentence is coming from a Harvard professor whose most famous students go on to run hedge funds. He says as much himself: more and more of his students arrive believing that a business career means buying, selling, and investing in companies, and he tells them that doing deals does not produce the reward that comes from building people up. The shelf spent a season on the ways organisations convert the second kind of work into the first without ever calling it that, promotion by performance into incompetence, blame kept vague so it never lands, indicators gamed until they measure nothing. Christensen's answer to his own students is not a refutation of any of that. It is a claim about where, inside the same organisations, the actual reward was hiding the whole time, for a manager willing to look for it there instead of on a balance sheet.

Chapter Five: The Strategy Nobody Chose

Before the theory of resource allocation, the article makes a quieter demand: that you first know what you are allocating toward. Christensen traces this back to the same Oxford years as the basketball story, a habit he built of spending an hour most nights reading, thinking, and praying about why he had been put on the earth, time taken directly from a doctoral program with no patience for it. He is candid that the trade felt indefensible most weeks; an hour not spent mastering the statistics of autocorrelation, in a field where autocorrelation was the whole exam, is an hour a supervisor would have called wasted. He kept at it anyway, and concluded decades later that he used the specific econometric techniques a handful of times a year for the rest of his career, and used what that hour gave him every single day instead. Without it, he says, a life sails off without a rudder, however much theory it is carrying. Everything the resource allocation chapter argues assumes this unglamorous first step: a purpose is what allocation gets measured against, and a plan with no destination is not deliberate, whatever the paper it is written on says.

The second question is where the book's argument stops being a motivational reading of an old theory and becomes something closer to a diagnosis, because the theory it borrows is one Christensen had spent years proving true of companies before he ever pointed it at a person. A firm's strategy, in his research, is not the document the board approves. It is whatever the resource allocation process actually funds, quarter after quarter, once the pressure of the moment gets to choose. A company can write down an ambitious long-term plan and still starve it, because every individual decision along the way goes to whichever project shows a return first, and the sum of ten thousand small, locally sensible choices adds up to a strategy nobody in the room ever voted for. Christensen calls the written plan the deliberate strategy and the thing that actually happens the emergent one, and the whole insight of his research career was that companies are usually run by the second, while congratulating themselves on the first.

He then does something few management theorists are willing to do in print, which is turn that finding on his own graduating class. Watching the reunions of his nineteen seventy-nine cohort roll by, he counted more and more of his former classmates arriving divorced, estranged from children they had once wanted badly enough to plan a family around. Not one of them, he says, walked out of Harvard with the deliberate strategy of ending up there. What happened instead was the emergent strategy: an achievement-driven person, handed an extra half hour or an extra ounce of energy, will spend it on whatever gives back a result you can point to today. You ship the product. You close the sale. You get the promotion. A marriage does not pay out on that schedule; a child does not hand you evidence you raised her well for another twenty years. So the hour goes to the thing that answers back, over and over, one defensible decision at a time, until the sum of them is a stranger at the dinner table.

I want to run one case through this, built rather than borrowed, because the mechanism is easiest to see in a life close to the shelf's own listener. A junior consultant tells herself, most weeks, that she will make it home for her daughter's bedtime once the grant application is in, or once this rotation ends, or once the paper is under review, and each single week the trade looks defensible: an hour tonight against a funding decision that could shape the next three years of her career, versus a bedtime story her daughter will not remember by name. Told once, the choice is obviously correct. Told fifty-two times a year for a decade, it is a strategy, chosen the way Christensen's theory says strategies actually get chosen, by ten thousand locally rational trades that nobody ever sat down to approve, and one day she looks up from a completed grant and finds a fifteen-year-old who has stopped waiting to be tucked in.

Chapter Six: Power Tools and the Family That Waited Too Long

The same section of the class supplies a second model, called the tools of cooperation, built to explain how a manager gets a team to move in the same direction. Where people agree neither on what they want nor on how to get it, the only lever that works is coercion: rules, threats, punishment, what Christensen calls power tools. Where agreement on both grows through repeated success, something more durable forms, a set of shared, unspoken instincts about how things get done here, which is what he means by a culture, and which no longer needs to be enforced because nobody in the room thinks to do it any other way.

Applied to a family, the model produces an uncomfortable timeline. Power tools work fine on small children; a four-year-old who is told no does, on the whole, stop. They stop working somewhere in adolescence, exactly when the stakes get highest, and by then it is too late to start building the culture that would have made the rule unnecessary. The culture had to be under construction years earlier, while the child was still small enough that a shared instinct about who this family is and what it does could be laid down through the low-stakes years, so that it was already strong enough to bear weight by the time the teenager needed it to hold without a parent standing over the decision.

The chapter's harder claim is a warning about outsourcing. A family that can afford it hands its children to tutors for algebra, coaches for the travel team, camps for leadership, on the reasonable theory that specialists will do each of those jobs better than a tired parent after work. Christensen's argument, borrowed from his own research on what makes a company capable of anything at all, is that a capability is never just the resources you can buy; it is also the internal processes a person has practiced and the priorities they have absorbed from watching what the adults around them actually reward, and neither of those transfers with a cheque. A child handed every experience pre-solved by a specialist never gets handed the harder, cheaper thing: a problem nobody has fixed for her yet, that she has to sit with until she works out what she is made of. The tutor can teach the algebra. Only the failed piano recital, sat through and recovered from at the family's own kitchen table, teaches the child what she does when something she tried does not work.

The book gives this a name borrowed straight from Christensen's corporate research: a capability, whether a company's or a child's, is built from resources, the raw material anyone with money can buy; processes, the practiced ways of turning material into something useful; and priorities, the values that decide what gets attempted at all. Parents shop almost exclusively in the first category, better school, better coach, better summer, and treat the other two as though they arrive on their own. They do not. A child's processes are built the same way an engineer's are, by doing a hard thing badly enough times to get it right, and her priorities are built by watching which of her parents' own stated values survive contact with an inconvenient Tuesday.

Chapter Seven: Ninety-Eight Percent

The third question, how to stay out of jail, gets its answer from a piece of first-year finance: when comparing two courses of action, ignore the sunk and fixed costs and weigh only the marginal ones, the cost of the next unit against the revenue it brings. It is sound doctrine for choosing between two machines. Applied to a life, Christensen argues, it becomes the mechanism by which honest people talk themselves into the thing they said they would never do. A voice explains that the general rule holds, as a rule, for other people, in ordinary circumstances; but this circumstance is different, and the cost of bending just this once looks small enough to absorb. It always looks small in the moment, because the marginal cost of one exception is, by definition, close to nothing. What it hides is the full cost of having become a person who bends.

He tells the story once, to its actual end, rather than as an illustration in passing. He played centre for the Oxford varsity basketball team during his Rhodes years, on a squad that went unbeaten through the season and reached the final of the British equivalent of the national championship, against the best friends he says he ever made. The final fell on a Sunday. At sixteen he had made a private commitment never to play sport on the Sabbath, and he told his coach he could not play. The coach did not believe him. His own teammates came to him one by one and asked him to break the rule this one time, for them, for the team that had worked all season for exactly this game. He went away, prayed on it, and did not play.

He calls it, looking back, the decision that shaped every year that followed, not for the game itself but for what would have followed had he crossed that line even once. His life, he says, turned out to be an unbroken stream of extenuating circumstances, each one arriving dressed as the exception that proved the rule; had he broken it that one Sunday, on grounds that felt sufficient at the time, he would have broken it every time after, because the grounds always feel sufficient at the time. The lesson he draws is closer to arithmetic than to piety: it is easier, in practice, to hold a line at one hundred percent of the time than at ninety-eight, because the moment a line admits one exception it has stopped being a line and become a negotiation, re-opened every time the pressure returns.

The shelf has met this exact mechanism from the other side already. Jackall's managers, back in the season built on Moral Mazes, survived inside their corporations by learning to keep every commitment conditional, to treat each ethical line as a negotiating position rather than a fact, because a manager who never bent was a manager who could not be promoted. Christensen is describing the identical trade from the inside of the person making it, one marginal exception at a time, and naming what Jackall's book left as an unstated cost: that the discount rate on your own integrity looks generous right up until the day you find out you have spent it all.

Chapter Eight: The Job You Were Hired For

The book's fourth model arrives almost as an aside, but it is the one that travelled furthest beyond the classroom, because it began as market research rather than moral philosophy. Christensen and a team of researchers had been hired to find out why a fast-food chain's milkshakes were not selling better, and after the usual approach, survey people who fit the profile of a milkshake buyer and ask what they wanted improved, failed to move sales at all, they tried something else: standing in the restaurant and simply watching who actually bought one, then asking each of them, afterward, what job they had hired the milkshake to do. Close to half the milkshakes sold before eight in the morning, to solitary commuters who wanted something that would last the whole drive to work, wasn't so thick it needed two hands, and left them a little less bored at a red light. The milkshake's real competitor most mornings was not another milkshake. It was a banana, a bagel, or nothing at all.

Christensen's extension of that idea to a marriage is stated almost too plainly to register as an argument: one of the largest jobs anyone is ever hired to do, in his own phrase, is to be a spouse, and most people take the job without ever asking what it actually requires, assuming instead that what they would want in the role is what their partner wants too. The mechanism is the same one that sank the milkshake redesign. A company that asks what customers say they want, rather than watching what problem they are actually trying to solve, improves the wrong thing convincingly. A spouse who assumes rather than asks does exactly that, for years, and calls the resulting loneliness a mystery.

Chapter Nine: The Case Against

The most serious objection to this book does not come from a reader who disliked it. It comes from the fate of the theory it borrows most heavily from, disruptive innovation itself, which by the time this book appeared had already been elevated from a research finding into something closer to a creed, cited to justify every start-up's contempt for every incumbent. In two thousand and fourteen the Harvard historian Jill Lepore published a long essay in the New Yorker arguing that the theory's own evidence did not hold up: several of the incumbent firms Christensen's original research had cast as doomed by disruption had gone on, in the years after his book about them, to perform perfectly well; the case selection, she argued, had a way of finding disruption wherever the author went looking for it, and missing the ordinary causes, in one famous instance a labour dispute at U.S. Steel, sitting in plain sight beside it. Her verdict on the whole apparatus was that it functioned less as a tested account of how industries actually change than as, in her words, a theory of history founded on a profound anxiety about financial collapse and shaky evidence.

That fight was about companies, not marriages, and Christensen's own defence of the underlying research is substantial enough that the argument is still unsettled. But it matters here for a reason the debate itself never raised: every model in this book, resource allocation, the tools of cooperation, jobs to be done, was built and tested the same way disruption theory was, against a portfolio of firms a researcher could compare to one another, firm against firm, industry against industry, looking for what the successes had in common that the failures lacked. A life offers no such comparison. Nobody gets to run their own marriage twice, once allocating the marginal hour to the office and once to the kitchen table, and check which strategy actually produced the twenty-year outcome. The clinician's instinct is to ask for the denominator before believing the numerator, and here there simply isn't one. Every case in this book is an n of one, examined after the fact by the very person whose life it was, the precise condition under which a compelling story is easiest to construct and hardest to falsify.

Christensen's own reaction to Lepore's essay makes the same point better than any critic could. Rather than answer with evidence, he told a Businessweek reporter he was angry that a scholar of her standing would commit, in his own words, a criminal act of dishonesty, and at Harvard of all places; he suggested she might simply have walked across campus and asked him first. It is the exact move his own book warns readers against in every other chapter, defending a position by asserting it harder rather than running it back through the evidence, and the fact that the man who built a career teaching executives to hear the counterargument could not sit still for one aimed at himself is, on its own, half the case against taking his self-examination on faith.

The other half is what several of the book's own readers flagged that its author never did. One reviewer, Russell Fox, wrote that he kept catching, page after page, a certain privilege and elitism in Christensen's assumptions that seemed to call for its own self-critique and never once got one. Another, a reader named Dorthe, pointed to a pattern running through the book's chosen examples: a steady preference for stay-at-home mothers, working fathers, and families of five or six children, presented as simply what a strong family looks like rather than as one option among many that happens to be the author's own. The outsourcing chapter is the clearest place this shows up. It tells the reader that hiring a tutor for algebra costs a child the chance to build her own capability, which is true as far as it goes, but the chapter never asks what it costs the family that has no choice but to work the extra shift instead of sitting with her at the kitchen table, because the shift is what keeps the lights on. The theory is not wrong. It is aimed, without ever admitting so, at a reader with slack in the system to spend, and the same clinician's habit that asks for the denominator should also ask what the check was built to miss.

Chapter Ten: Verdict, Dose, and a Question

The book ends where it must, with the fact that made the whole project urgent rather than theoretical. In the year before the article that started it, Christensen had been told he might not have much life left to measure. He writes, near the close, that a diagnosis like that has an efficient way of clarifying what the metrics were ever for; he had a clear enough sense of how much revenue his ideas had generated for the companies that used them, and found, confronting the possibility of dying, that the number meant almost nothing to him. The yardstick he settled on instead was not dollars. It was the individual people whose lives had been better for having crossed his.

The verdict is that this is the most personally useful book on the shelf's antidote season, and also its least self-aware, and that both of those things are true for the same reason: a researcher who spent a career finding the blind spots in other people's strategies never quite manages to find his own. Read the ten-page article first, since the whole argument is already there and none of the book's length adds a fifth idea. Then read the chapters on resource allocation and the ninety-eight percent rule twice, because they are the two genuine mechanisms in the book, the ones that would survive even if every anecdote around them were struck out. Read the parenting chapter once, and then read Fox's review beside it, because the chapter is more useful once you know whose kitchen table it was written at.

The dose is a caution the shelf has not needed to give before. This is not a cynical book that poisons in large amounts; it is a warm one whose flattery works the same way at any dose, and the risk is not that the reader takes it too seriously but that they take its examples as the template rather than the case study, and go looking for the version of a good life that happens to look like Christensen's own.

The question to carry into the coming week is his, sharpened by everything the case against found missing from it. Name the one place this week where your calendar's actual strategy and your stated one had already parted ways, the hour that went to what would answer back today over what would only answer back in twenty years. Then ask a second question the book never thought to ask on your behalf: who paid the marginal cost of that hour, and did they get a vote.

Next time, the shelf leaves the antidote season behind and goes looking for a mechanism that keeps discovering itself under new names: the measurement constellation, a nineteen fifty-six paper by a forgotten researcher named Ridgway who watched performance targets warp the very things they measured, rediscovered nineteen years later by Goodhart and again, four years after that, by Campbell, each one certain he was first. Thanks for listening.

item.title: High Output Management (Grove): leverage, one-on-ones, and what a manager produces
item.description: Andy Grove's 1983 manual as the third antidote – the breakfast factory, the limiting step, leverage, the one-on-one, task-relevant maturity as the answer to the Peter Principle, paired indicators, and why the book reads like a factory floor because it came from one.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Three-Minute Egg

Grove opens his book with breakfast, and I will too, because it is the best teaching example on this shelf and he wrote it in nineteen eighty-three for people who ran wafer fabs. You are a waiter, and your job is to deliver a breakfast of a soft-boiled egg, buttered toast, and coffee, hot, together, on time. The egg takes three minutes to boil. The toast takes a minute or so. The coffee is already made. What do you do first? You start the egg, because the egg is the limiting step, the operation that takes longest and that everything else must be arranged around. You put the bread in while the egg boils, and you pour the coffee last, so that all three land on the tray together. Production management in one paragraph, and Grove spends the next twenty pages getting more out of it: what happens when the egg-boiler breaks and you have to buy eggs pre-boiled, which costs more but saves capacity; what a customer waiting in line represents in inventory; where in the process you would inspect, and whether inspecting every egg is worth it, or whether you should sample. Then he scales it. The breakfast factory serves a thousand breakfasts an hour. Now the egg is a continuous boiler, the toast is a conveyor, and the questions are the same, and they are the questions of the plant he actually ran.

The question this book answers, and the reason it belongs in the shelf's antidote season, is this: what does a manager produce? The cynical canon spent a month answering that question from the outside, and the answers were blame, cover, retinue, and paperwork. Grove's answer is from the inside, and it is a formula. A manager's output is the output of the organisation under him plus the output of the neighbouring organisations under his influence. Nothing the manager does with his own hands counts. Only what the people under him make. And from that formula follows everything else in the book, including the parts that will make a hospital manager wince.

Chapter Two: Who He Was

András Gróf was born in Budapest in nineteen thirty-six to a Jewish family. He survived scarlet fever at four, which left him nearly deaf; he survived the German occupation, hidden with his mother under a false name while his father was in a labour battalion; and he survived the Soviet siege. In nineteen fifty-six, when the Russians put down the uprising, he walked across the border into Austria at twenty, with the clothes he stood in, and reached New York the following January. He learned English, took a chemical engineering degree at City College while working as a busboy, and a doctorate at Berkeley, and joined Fairchild Semiconductor in sixty-three. When Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore left Fairchild five years later to found Intel, Grove was their first hire. He ran the operations for two decades, became president in seventy-nine and chief executive in eighty-seven, and by the time he stepped down in ninety-eight Intel made the processor in most of the world's computers. Time magazine made him its man of the year in ninety-seven. He wrote a memoir of the Hungarian years, Swimming Across, and a second management book, Only the Paranoid Survive, and he died in twenty sixteen.

The biography is in the book in one way that a reader should know about. Grove came to management as a physical chemist with a hearing aid, and he treated it as an engineering problem: a set of processes with inputs, throughputs, limiting steps, and measurable outputs. That is the book's strength and the whole of the case against it, and I will come back to both. For now, hold onto the fact that a manual on management written by a refugee who had been a busboy contains not one page about ambition, politics, or self-presentation. Whyte's organization man, from episodes six to eight, spent his career managing his image. Grove's manager spends it managing a fab.

Chapter Three: Leverage

Once the manager's output is defined as the output of the team, the manager's problem becomes one of allocation: where does an hour of the manager's time produce the largest increase in the team's output? Grove's word for that is leverage, and the book is a catalogue of high-leverage and low-leverage activities. A manager who spends an hour training a new member of staff who will then work for a year at a higher level has produced, on Grove's arithmetic, something like two hundred hours of improved output from a single hour of input. A manager who spends the same hour redoing a subordinate's work, because he can do it faster, has produced sixty minutes of output and taught the subordinate that the work will be redone. The first is leverage. The second is what most managers do most of the day.

He is specific about negative leverage, and this is the section I would give to any new consultant. A manager who is depressed depresses the people around him, and their output falls; a manager who is late to his own meetings costs each attendee the waiting time, so a manager who is ten minutes late to a meeting of eight people has spent an hour and twenty minutes of the organisation's time; a manager who interrupts is the highest-leverage negative activity there is, because an interruption does not cost the interrupted person the minute it takes, it costs them the twenty minutes it takes to get back to where they were. Grove's remedy for the last is what he calls batching: the manager sets aside fixed times when interruptions are welcome, and in return is left alone the rest of the time. The hospital equivalent is the consultant who is available at the board round and the afternoon huddle and unreachable in between, and whose juniors, after a week of it, have learned to save their questions and ask better ones.

The idea of leverage carries an implication that Grove states and most managers avoid: the manager's calendar is the manager's output. Every hour spent in a meeting that did not need him, every report read that changed no decision, every task done personally that a subordinate could have done, is output the team did not get. The shelf spent an episode on Parkinson's law, that work expands to fill the time available; Grove is the practitioner's reply, that a manager who knows what his output is can tell when the expansion is happening, because it shows up as hours spent at low leverage.

Chapter Four: The Meeting Is the Work

Grove's second heresy, for a reader raised on the belief that meetings are where work goes to die, is that meetings are the medium in which managerial work is done, the way the operating theatre is the medium of surgery. The mistake is to treat all meetings as one thing. He divides them in two. The process-oriented meeting is regular, scheduled, and expected: the one-on-one, the staff meeting, the operations review. The mission-oriented kind is called to make a specific decision and should be rare, because it is expensive and because if you need a lot of them your process meetings are failing.

The one-on-one is the centre of the book, and it is the practice that Silicon Valley took from Grove and that most hospitals have never heard of. The manager meets each direct subordinate, alone, regularly, for an hour or so. The subordinate sets the agenda and does most of the talking. The manager's job is to listen, to coach, and, above all, to learn what is going on, because the one-on-one is the manager's best source of the information his formula depends on. Grove's instruction to the manager is that when the subordinate has finished on a topic, ask one more question, since the thing the subordinate did not intend to mention is usually behind the last answer. He is exact about frequency: weekly for a subordinate new to the job or the task, fortnightly or monthly for the experienced one, and he calls the meeting the subordinate's meeting, not the manager's. The hour belongs to the person being managed. I know of no hospital that runs this. Consultants see their registrars on the ward round, in a crowd, with the patient present, and the annual appraisal is the only scheduled hour they will ever spend alone, and it is spent filling in a form. Grove would say the hospital has decided not to know what its people know.

He has a set of rules for the decision meeting that are worth carrying too, because they answer the shelf's Jackall problem directly. Jackall's managers, from the first episode, kept decisions vague so that blame had nowhere to land. Grove's rule is that before the meeting ends the group must know what decision was made, who will act on it, by when, and, if the decision was not made, when it will be. The decision is to be made at the lowest level competent to make it, by the people closest to the information, and the more senior people in the room are to keep quiet until the junior ones have spoken, since a senior view expressed early ends the discussion. He calls the whole thing the ideal decision-making process, and he is candid that Intel did not always manage it. The difference from Jackall's world is that at Intel the failure to reach a decision was counted as a failure.

Chapter Five: Task-Relevant Maturity, and the Answer to Peter

Here is the chapter that the shelf has been waiting for since episode thirteen. Laurence Peter's principle, that every employee rises to their level of incompetence, was the funniest book on the cynical shelf and the one whose mechanism the shelf found most robust: promotion by performance in the current job guarantees eventual promotion into a job the person cannot do. Grove read Peter, and he agrees with the mechanism, and his answer is not to abandon promoting on performance, because he can see no alternative, but to change what a manager does with the person who has just been promoted.

The tool is what he calls task-relevant maturity, and it is a claim that the right way to manage someone depends on how well they can do the specific task in front of them, not on their competence in general. A superb engineer moved into a manager's job has low task-relevant maturity in management on Monday morning, whatever her maturity as an engineer, and she should be managed the way a beginner is managed: with close structure, clear instructions, frequent check-ins, the weekly one-on-one. As she gains maturity in the task, the structure comes off, and the same manager manages her by objectives, then by little more than occasional conversation. Then she is moved to a new task, or the task changes under her, and the structure goes back on. The management style tracks the person's competence at the task, and it changes both ways.

Read that against Peter. Peter's promoted employee fails because the organisation, having promoted her on the strength of her old competence, manages her as if she still had it. It leaves her alone. Grove's promoted employee is managed as the novice she now is, and either learns the new job under structure or is found out early, in the one-on-one, before the failure becomes the department's. And Grove adds the second half of the answer, which is about what happens to the ones who are found out. He calls it recycling, and he argues that moving a person back to the level at which they performed well should carry no disgrace, because the alternative, leaving them in the job they cannot do because a demotion would embarrass everyone, is exactly Peter's final placement. Intel, he says, did this, and the person often flourished. Whether it is possible in a hospital, where a step down in title is a public event and the professional culture treats it as a wound, is a question the book cannot answer, but at least it names the problem as one of the organisation's courage rather than the employee's ceiling.

Chapter Six: Indicators, and the Gaming of Them

The book's chapter on measurement is the one that will matter most to a clinician, and I want to read it against the shelf's long argument about targets. Grove ran a factory, so he measured everything: output per shift, yield, inventory, defects. He knew what happens when you measure one thing, which is that people produce that thing and let everything else go. His rule was that every indicator be paired with a second indicator that measures its opposite failure. Measure the number of vouchers processed by an accounts clerk and you will get many vouchers processed badly; so pair it with the count of errors found. Measure the inventory level and stockouts follow; pair it with the frequency of stockouts. Measure the janitor's square feet cleaned and pair it with an inspection of the rooms.

A hospital manager will recognise the failure the pairing is meant to prevent, because the health service has lived through it. Measure the four-hour wait in the emergency department and you get patients moved into corridors at three hours fifty-nine, or held in ambulances outside the door so the clock has not started. Measure length of stay and the result is discharges at eight in the evening with no transport home. Every one of those is an unpaired indicator, and the shelf will come to the theorists of that failure, Ridgway, Goodhart and Campbell, in an episode of their own. What Grove offers is the practitioner's version, from a decade before Campbell's law had a name in management: the measured thing will be produced, so measure two things that cannot both be gamed in the same direction. The four-hour wait paired with the rate of readmission within a week. Length of stay paired with the discharge-hour distribution. It is not a complete defence, because a clever enough organisation can game two indicators, and Grove's own book makes the point that the indicator is a tool for the manager's attention and not a substitute for it. But it is the difference between an organisation that has thought about gaming and one that has published a target and awaited the consequences.

Grove's other contribution to measurement is the one the Valley later took from him and renamed. He describes Intel's system of management by objectives, in which each person has a small number of objectives for the quarter, each with key results by which it can be seen to have been met or not, and the objectives at each level are derived from the level above. He is emphatic that the number must be few, since a person with ten objectives has none, and that the key results must be things that can be checked, not aspirations. John Doerr, who worked at Intel under Grove, carried the method to Google in nineteen ninety-nine, and it has spread under the name objectives and key results to most of the technology industry and, in the last decade, to hospitals. Grove's own chapter on it is shorter and better than the books that followed, and it contains a warning the followers dropped: the objectives system is a tool for focusing attention, and when it becomes a tool for evaluation, when people are paid by their key results, the pairing problem returns, because now the results will be gamed.

Chapter Seven: The Door

The book's sequel is the best evidence for the book, and I want to spend a chapter on it, because it shows the methods under load. In nineteen eighty-five Intel was a memory company. It had invented the dynamic random-access memory chip and built the firm on it, and by the mid-eighties the Japanese manufacturers were making the same chips better and cheaper, and Intel was losing money on every one. Grove tells the story in Only the Paranoid Survive, from ninety-six. He was in his office with Gordon Moore, the co-founder and then chairman, and he asked him a question: if the board threw them both out and brought in a new chief executive, what would that person do? Moore said the new man would get Intel out of memories. Grove's reply was that in that case they should walk out of the door, come back in, and do it themselves.

Two things about that story belong on this shelf. The first is that the decision had, in Grove's account, already been made by the people below him. Intel's production planners had been shifting wafer capacity from memory to the microprocessor for over a year, on the arithmetic of the margins, without any strategic announcement, so that by the time the executives decided to leave the memory business the factories had half-left already. Grove calls the middle managers who see the change first the Cassandras, and the chapter is a plea to listen to them: the one-on-one from the first book, applied to the survival of the firm. The people who knew were the people with low rank and high contact with the data, and the organisation's job was to let their knowledge move upward before it was too late. That is Hirschman's voice mechanism, run inside a company that had built the channels for it.

The second is the walk to the door. Grove's insight was that he and Moore could not make the decision as themselves, because the memory business was their identity, and that the way to make it was to imagine themselves replaced. It is an exit-and-re-entry, in Hirschman's vocabulary, performed inside one afternoon, and it is the most practical trick in either book. A clinical director who cannot close a service she built, a research group that cannot drop the line of work that got it funded, a department that cannot stop a clinic nobody attends, all need the door. The question is what a stranger, appointed tomorrow with no history here, would do on their first morning, and then whether there is any honest reason not to do it today.

The sequel also records a failure, and Grove's handling of it is the best short case in management I know for the idea that the manager's output is the organisation's. In ninety-four a mathematician in Virginia found that the Pentium processor divided certain numbers wrongly, at the ninth decimal place, in about one calculation in nine billion. Intel's engineers, correctly on the numbers, judged that no ordinary user would ever encounter it, and the company's first response was to replace the chip only for customers who could show they needed the precision. The response was a technical answer to what had become a trust question, and it was destroyed on the internet and in the newspapers within weeks; IBM stopped shipping Pentium machines; and Intel wrote off four hundred and seventy-five million dollars to replace every chip on request. Grove's own account is that he had missed the change from a company selling components to engineers who understood a defect rate to one selling a brand to people who did not, and that his indicators, all of which were engineering indicators, could not show it. The pairing rule from the first book had been broken by its author: the defect rate had no partner measuring what the customer believed. He learned it at the cost of half a billion dollars and wrote it down, and the writing down is why I trust him on the rest.

Chapter Eight: The Case Against

The objections to this book divide into complaints about its style and objections to its world. The style objection is the one every reader makes: the book reads like a manufacturing manual, because it is one, and the metaphors of the fab, throughput, yield, inventory, inspection, sit awkwardly on work that is not a fab. A Goodreads reviewer's complaint that the task-relevant maturity chapter could have been one sentence, learn about your subordinates so that you know how to manage them, is unfair to the chapter and fair to the tone. And the maturity idea itself is not Grove's; it is a restatement of the situational leadership model that Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard had published in the seventies, which Grove acknowledges in passing, and which the academic literature has found hard to confirm in controlled studies. Grove's contribution was to show it working in a company, which is evidence of a kind, and not the kind the model's critics were asking for.

The world objection is more serious. Grove's manager is a manager of engineers making a physical product with a measurable yield, in a company where the people under him reported to him, where he set their objectives and could move them between jobs. The book has no theory of the professional who does not report to the manager, and so it has nothing to say about a hospital. A clinical director does not set the consultants' objectives, cannot recycle one of them to a lesser post, and cannot run a one-on-one as the subordinate's meeting with a colleague who is not a subordinate. Grove's leverage arithmetic assumes an authority that the medical director does not have, and a manager who applies the book without noticing this will spend a year wondering why the fab metaphors have produced resentment and no throughput.

And then there is Intel. The company Grove built did, for twenty years after his book, exactly what he said a well-managed organisation would do. It also, in the two decades after he left, missed the mobile processor, fell behind in fabrication technology for the first time in its history, and lost the position that Grove's methods had won. Ben Horowitz, who wrote the foreword to the twenty fifteen reissue and did more than anyone to make the book a Valley scripture, would say that the methods were abandoned, not refuted. I think that is probably right, and I think it concedes something Grove did not say: that a management system is only as durable as the manager who insists on it, and that the book contains no mechanism for making it survive him. The shelf's cynical canon was, among other things, a study of what happens to good systems after the founder goes. Grove's book is a study of the founder's system. Both are true. The second does not answer the first.

Chapter Nine: What a Clinician Can Take

Set the fab metaphors aside and what is left is a small number of practices that the shelf's diagnosis says a hospital needs and that a hospital can actually run. The first is the formula. A consultant who has just become a clinical director and still thinks of her output as her clinics and her lists has not yet become a manager, and the fastest way to become one is to ask, every week, what the department produced and what she did that made it produce more. Most of what she did will fail that test, and the failing items are where the leverage is hiding.

The second is the one-on-one, run as Grove describes it, the subordinate's agenda and the manager listening, and I will constrain it to the relationship where it can actually be run: the consultant and her registrars. Half an hour, fortnightly, alone, no form, the registrar talks. It would be the only hour in the training in which someone senior heard what the junior actually thought was going wrong, and the shelf's whole Hirschman episode was about the cost of not having that hour. The third is the pairing of indicators, and any manager who reports a number can do it from tomorrow: for every metric that goes to the board, name the way it will be gamed, and report the metric that would catch the gaming beside it.

And the fourth is the answer to Peter, the one that costs the most. The department's newly promoted registrar, the new consultant, the new lead, has low task-relevant maturity in the new job whatever they were before, and the kindness of leaving them alone is Peter's mechanism at work. The structure goes on for the first year. It comes off when the maturity is there. Grove would add that the person who does not get there should be allowed a way back that is not a humiliation, and that the organisation which cannot offer one has chosen Peter's final placement for its own convenience.

Chapter Ten: Verdict, Dose, and a Question

The verdict is that this is the most useful book on the shelf for a person who has just been put in charge of something, and that it should be read with its world in mind. Read the twenty fifteen edition, with Horowitz's foreword and Grove's own preface from ninety-five, which adds the parts about email and the middle manager's exposure to the market that the eighty-three edition did not have. Read chapters one and two, the breakfast factory, first, because the whole method is in them. Read the one-on-one chapter twice. Skip nothing, since the book is short, but read the chapter on interviewing with the knowledge that hospitals do not hire the way fabs do.

The dose is different from the shelf's usual warning, and different from Ostrom's too. Grove is not poison at any dose, but he is a drug with a specific indication, which is a manager who has the authority his methods assume. A reader without that authority who takes the whole book will try to run a fab in a building full of people who do not work for her, and the book will get the blame for the result. Take the formula, the one-on-one, the paired indicator, and the maturity idea, and leave the throughput arithmetic to the people with a throughput.

The question to carry into the week is Grove's own, and it is the best single management question I know. Take your calendar for last week and, for each hour, ask what the output of your team was increased by that hour. Not what you did; what they produced because of it. The hours that have no answer are the hours in which you were not managing, and there will be more of them than you can comfortably count, and the arithmetic, once done, is hard to un-know.

Next time, the fourth and last antidote, and the one that turns the shelf's instruments on the reader's own life: Clayton Christensen's How Will You Measure Your Life?, from the last class he taught his Harvard students each year, on what a theory of business has to say about a career, a family, and staying out of jail. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Governing the Commons (Ostrom): how communities run shared resources without the state
item.description: Elinor Ostrom's 1990 book as the second antidote – Hardin's tragedy, the Swiss village that has grazed one alp since 1483, the Valencia water court, the fisheries that failed, the eight design principles, and what a hospital's shared things have in common with a pasture.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Pasture Everybody Knows

In nineteen sixty-eight the biologist Garrett Hardin published a short essay in Science with a title that has done more work than its argument. The Tragedy of the Commons. You know the picture even if you have never read it, because it is taught in the first week of every economics course and half the environmental ones. A pasture is open to all. Each herdsman gains the whole benefit of adding one more animal and bears only a fraction of the cost, since the overgrazing is shared. So each adds another, and another, and the pasture is destroyed, and no one could have done otherwise. Hardin's conclusion was that the only escapes were privatisation, which gives each herdsman his own fenced field and his own consequences, or coercion, which gives the state the whip. Freedom in a commons, he wrote, brings ruin to all.

The essay was about population, the part everybody forgets, and it recommended coercion on that subject too. But the pasture escaped the essay and became a fact about the world. For twenty years after it appeared, policy toward every shared resource on earth, forests, fisheries, groundwater, grazing land, was argued from that picture, and the argument was always between the two escapes: sell it, or nationalise it. Governments in Nepal nationalised the village forests in nineteen fifty-seven, and the forests, which had been managed by the villages for generations, were stripped in a decade, because a forest that belongs to the state in Kathmandu belongs to nobody on the hillside. Fisheries were privatised into tradeable quotas. Both escapes were taken, all over the world, on the strength of a two-page parable that contained no data.

Elinor Ostrom's contribution, in the plainest terms, was to go and look. Governing the Commons, from nineteen ninety, is a report on what she found, and what she found was that the pasture in the essay does not exist. Real pastures have people on them, and the people talk, and over centuries they have worked out, without a landlord and without a state, how to keep the grass. This episode is about what those arrangements look like, why some fail, the eight properties the durable ones share, and what the shelf, after a season of watching institutions fail, should make of a book whose subject is institutions that work.

Chapter Two: Who She Was

Ostrom was born Elinor Awan in Los Angeles in nineteen thirty-three, to a family that the Depression had made poor. She stuttered as a child and was put on the debate team to fix it, which she later credited with teaching her that every question has two defensible sides and that the job is to find out which one the evidence favours. She wanted a doctorate in economics at the University of California at Los Angeles and was refused, because she had not taken the trigonometry that the department required and, as a woman, had been steered away from it in school. She took political science instead, where the entrance exam was easier and the faculty told her openly that a woman would be wasting a place. Her doctoral work, in the early sixties, was on the groundwater basins under Los Angeles, which were being pumped faster than they refilled, and which the users, cities and water companies and farmers, had organised themselves to save through a mixture of litigation, negotiated quotas, and a new taxing district. She watched a commons being governed, in the middle of a city, by its own users, thirty years before she wrote the book. Everything after was an attempt to find out whether what she had seen in Los Angeles was general.

With her husband Vincent she built a research group at Indiana University that they called the Workshop, and the name was a statement. Research there was a craft, done in collaboration, on cases, with the theory revised every time a case broke it. She sent students to Nepal and Kenya and the Philippines and taught them a coding protocol so that a forest in one country could be compared with a forest in another. In two thousand and nine she was awarded the Nobel Prize in economics, the first woman to receive it, shared with Oliver Williamson, and the citation named the thing she had shown: that common property can be successfully managed by the people who use it. She died in two thousand and twelve, and the last piece she published, that same year, was on the same subject as the first.

Chapter Three: Törbel, and the Rule About Winter

The book's method is to take the cases first and the theory after, and I will follow it. The first case is a village in the Swiss canton of Valais called Törbel, six hundred people, on a mountainside, and the reason it is in the book is that its records go back to fourteen eighty-three. In that year the villagers signed a document establishing an association to govern their common land, the alp where the cows grazed in summer, the forests where they cut timber and firewood, the waste land, the irrigation channels, and the paths. Private property existed alongside: each family owned its own fields and vineyards and hay meadows in the valley. What was held in common was what could not usefully be divided, the high pasture that is only good for grazing for a few months, and the forest whose value depends on being managed as one.

The rule that governed the alp is the one to remember, because it is so simple and so hard to think of. No villager could send more cows to the summer pasture than he could feed through the winter from his own hay. Hardin's herdsman adds an animal because the pasture is free. Törbel's herdsman cannot, because the number of animals he may graze is tied to a resource he owns and pays for, his winter hay, and the tie is checked in public every year when the cows go up. The rule uses the private property to ration the common one. The village elected officials to count the cows and impose the fines, kept the fines in the community's own accounts, and used the money for the paths and the channels. The forest was managed by the same association: trees were marked for felling by the officials, the felled timber was divided by lot among the households, and no one cut what had not been marked.

Ostrom is careful to say what this is not. It is not an unmanaged commons, in Hardin's sense. Nobody in Törbel could walk onto the alp with a herd. It is not private property either; the alp was never divided, and the association that owned it had no owner. And it is not the state: the canton and the confederation left the villagers to it. It is a third thing, and the book's argument is that this third thing is everywhere once you look, and that the two-escapes framing had made it invisible. The Japanese villages that Margaret McKean studied, with their common mountain land and their rules about how much grass each household could cut, and the day each spring when the cutting was opened, and the patrols that caught the early cutters, are the same institution in a different language. So are the Philippine irrigation societies, the zanjeras, in which the labour of maintaining the canal is owed in proportion to the water received, and a member who fails to turn up for the maintenance day loses water in proportion.

Chapter Four: The Water Court at the Cathedral Door

The second case is the one I would send a sceptic to, because it is still running and you can go and watch. In the huerta of Valencia, the irrigated plain around the city, farmers have shared the water of the Turia river for something like a thousand years, through a system of canals with Arabic names, and the disputes between them are settled by a court called the Tribunal de las Aguas. It sits every Thursday at noon outside the Apostles' door of the cathedral. The judges are farmers, elected by the irrigators of each canal. There are no lawyers and no written record; a complaint is heard, the accused answers, and the judges rule on the spot, in Valencian, in public. The fines are small and the judgements have never, in the tribunal's recorded history, been appealed to a state court, which is a way of saying that the farmers regard it as theirs.

What Ostrom draws from the huerta is the mechanism of monitoring. Water in a canal system is stolen by taking it out of turn, or leaving your gate open longer than your allotted time. The person best placed to see that happen is the farmer whose turn is next, because it is his water that has gone. So the monitoring is done by the users, in the course of using, at no cost to anyone, and it is backed by a court that the users run and that meets within days. The huerta's system has an official, the guard of each canal, but the guard is not a policeman; he is the man the next farmer complains to. The sanction is graduated: a first offence is a small fine and public embarrassment, a repeat is larger, a persistent offender can lose his water. The graduation is not there for deterrence in the criminal-law sense. Its purpose is that the first fine is small enough that a farmer who has taken water in a dry year because his crop was dying, and everyone knows it, can be fined without being ruined, and can go on being a member. The rule is enforced, and the community survives the enforcement.

There is a detail from the neighbouring huertas that I like more than any other in the book. In Murcia and Orihuela, further south, the water is scarcer, and the rules are more elaborate; in Alicante, scarcer still, the water rights were separated from the land in the thirteenth century and are auctioned. The institutions vary with the scarcity, and vary in the direction a designer would choose, and no designer chose them. The people who needed them built them, one dispute at a time, over centuries, and they fit the river the way a glove fits a hand because they were shaped on the hand. The shelf met this idea last month in James Scott's mētis, the local practical knowledge that the high modernist cannot see. Ostrom's cases are what mētis looks like when it has been institutionalised, written down, and given a court.

Chapter Five: The Ones That Failed

A book containing only successful commons would prove nothing, and Ostrom knew it, so a third of hers is about failure. The Turkish fisheries are the cleanest comparison because they hold the culture, the law, and the fish constant and vary only the institution. At Alanya, on the Mediterranean coast, a hundred fishermen had spent the early nineteen seventies fighting over the best spots, with violence, rising costs, and falling catches, until the local cooperative devised a system: a list of the good fishing locations was drawn up, the eligible fishermen were listed, and in September each year they drew lots for their starting spots and then rotated daily, eastward, through the list. The rotation meant that every boat got every good spot in turn, so nobody had to fight for one, and it meant that a boat in the wrong spot was instantly visible to the boat that should have been there, so the monitoring was free. The system was not written into national law. It was enforced by the fishermen and, occasionally, by the coffee house.

At Bodrum and in Izmir Bay it went the other way. The number of boats was too large and too fluid, the government's development loans had brought in trawlers and outsiders with no stake in the local rules, and the fishermen never managed to agree who was in and who was out. Without a boundary there was no group to make a rule, and without a rule there was nothing to monitor, and the fisheries declined the way Hardin said they would. Ostrom's reading is that Hardin's tragedy is real, and that it happens in a specific condition: where the users cannot communicate, cannot define who belongs, and cannot make their own rules stick. Where those conditions are absent, so is the tragedy. Hardin's parable described a special case and sold it as a law.

She adds the Sri Lankan irrigation schemes, where the state built the canals and appointed the officials and the farmers stole the water and broke the gates, because the rules were Colombo's and the water was theirs; and the Nova Scotia inshore fisheries, where a functioning local system was overridden by a national licensing regime that treated the coast as one fishery; and the Californian groundwater basins where negotiation failed. The pattern of failure is consistent, and it is often the state's arrival, with good intentions and a general rule, that breaks a local arrangement that had been working. That is Scott's argument from below, and Ostrom got there first, with a more modest claim and better data.

Chapter Six: The Laboratory, and the Canals Nobody Built

Ostrom did one more thing that separates her from every other author on this shelf: she took the field cases into a laboratory and tried to break them. With Roy Gardner and James Walker, through the eighties and into the nineties, she ran experiments in which students at Indiana played a commons game for real money. Each player chose how much to invest in a shared resource whose return fell as total investment rose, the pasture in numbers, and the theory predicted that they would overinvest until the joint return was destroyed. On the first runs they did. Then the experimenters allowed the players to talk to each other, for a few minutes, with nothing enforceable, what game theory calls cheap talk because it should change nothing. It changed nearly everything. Groups that could communicate cut their overinvestment by most of the distance to the optimum and stayed there for round after round. Then the experimenters let the players fine each other, at a cost to the fining player, and the groups that could both talk and sanction did better still, while the ones who could only sanction without talking punished each other into a worse outcome than silence. The experiments are written up in Rules, Games, and Common-Pool Resources, from nineteen ninety-four, and what they show is that Hardin's result depends on a condition he did not state: that the herdsmen never meet.

This is the answer to an objection I will raise properly in a moment, about old, small, trusting communities. The students in the laboratory had met an hour earlier. They had no history, no shared church, and no expectation of seeing each other again, and a few minutes of talk was enough to move them most of the way to the villagers' outcome. Trust in those rooms was manufactured by the rules of the room, in the time it took to hold a conversation, and that is the claim a hospital department needs, because it has no five hundred years and it does have a meeting room.

The second piece of evidence is from Nepal, and it is the one I would put in front of anyone who still believes the state's engineers must know best. In the nineties the Workshop compiled data on more than a hundred irrigation systems in the Nepalese hills, some built and run by government agencies with concrete headworks and permanent canals, and some built by the farmers themselves out of stone, mud, and brush that had to be rebuilt after every monsoon. Wai Fung Lam's analysis of the data, published in nineteen ninety-eight, found that the farmer-managed systems delivered more water to the tail end of the canal, had higher cropping intensities, and kept their channels in better repair than the agency systems with the superior engineering. The mechanism is the one from the huerta. In a farmer-run system the people at the head of the canal need the people at the tail to turn up for the annual rebuilding, so they cannot take all the water; in the agency system the concrete does not need anyone, and the head-enders take what they like. The better technology broke the institution that made the water reach the end. The shelf spent two episodes last month on James Scott's argument that the state's improvements destroy what they cannot see. Here it is in litres.

Chapter Seven: The Eight Properties

The theory, when it comes, is not a model. It is a list of the properties that the durable cases share and the failed cases lack, and Ostrom calls them design principles while insisting that nobody designed them. There are eight, and for the ear I will give them as the questions a user of a shared resource would ask.

Who is in? The successful commons have a clear boundary, both of the resource and of the people entitled to use it. Do the rules fit this place? The rules for taking match the local conditions, the winter hay, the Thursday turn, the September rotation, and they match the rules for contributing. Who makes the rules? The people affected by them can take part in changing them. Who watches? The monitors are the users themselves or people answerable to them. What happens when someone breaks a rule? The sanctions are graduated, small for a first offence, larger for persistence. Where do disputes go? There is a cheap, fast, local place to settle them, the cathedral door. Will the outside let us? The state at least does not challenge the community's right to organise. And, for the big systems, are there layers? Appropriation, monitoring, enforcement, and dispute resolution are organised in nested units, the canal within the district within the river.

The principles have been the subject of a large empirical literature since, and I will come to it, but I want to draw out what they have in common, because it is not what a reader expecting a theory would expect. None of them is about incentives in the economist's sense, and none is about virtue. They are about information and about proportion. A boundary tells you whose behaviour to watch; user-monitoring makes the watching free; graduated sanctions make the first enforcement cheap enough to actually happen; the local court means the enforcement is fast enough to matter. Every principle reduces the cost of somebody finding out what somebody else did and doing something small about it, soon. Hardin's herdsman overgrazes because nothing he does is seen and nothing that is seen has a consequence. Ostrom's villagers do not, because everything is seen and the consequence is a fine on Thursday.

Chapter Eight: The Case Against

The objections come from two directions, and the more damaging one is friendly. Arun Agrawal, a scholar of forest commons, argued in two thousand and one that the design-principles literature, Ostrom's and the two other major lists that appeared around the same time, had between them produced more than thirty conditions said to matter for success, and that a theory with thirty variables and a few dozen cases cannot be tested; any case can be explained after the fact by whichever conditions it happens to display. That is the clinician's objection to a prognostic model with more predictors than patients, and it is correct. The reply came in two thousand and ten from Michael Cox, Gwen Arnold, and Sergio Villamayor-Tomás, who coded ninety-one published case studies and found that each of the principles, taken one at a time, was associated with success, and that the principles held up better when two of them, the boundaries one and the congruence one, were split into their components, making eleven. That study has itself been criticised, for taking the case authors' judgement of success at face value and for treating outcomes as one thing when they are ecological in one study and social in the next. I read the exchange as a field in the ordinary condition of a young science: a proposed set of predictors, one meta-analysis in favour, the meta-analysis under review. The principles survive as a checklist that the evidence has not contradicted, which is more than can be said for the parable they replaced.

The second objection is about scale, and Eduardo Araral put it plainly in two thousand and fourteen. Ostrom's cases are small: villages, a coast, a river plain. The commons that now matter, the atmosphere, the oceans, the antibiotic pool, are enormous, their users cannot meet, and the boundary cannot be drawn. Her principles, he argued, may be true of the Swiss alp and useless for the climate. Ostrom's own answer, in a paper for the World Bank in two thousand and nine, was the idea she called polycentric governance: that a global commons can be governed by many overlapping units at many scales, each doing what it can, rather than by a single global agreement, and that waiting for the treaty is itself a way of ensuring the tragedy. Whether that answer works is a question about the next fifty years, and I will not pretend to know. What I will say is that the objection concedes the book. Araral's complaint is that the principles do not scale, which grants that at the scale she studied they hold.

There is a third objection I want to raise myself, because it is the one this shelf is equipped to make. Ostrom's successful commons are old, small, and homogeneous. Törbel had six hundred people who had intermarried for five centuries. The huerta's farmers were Valencian Catholics who had shared a language and a calendar since the Reconquista. The design principles may be the visible surface of something harder to transplant, which is a community that already trusts itself, and a hospital department assembled from people who arrived last year and will leave next year is not that. I think this is a real limit, and I think the book's own cases, and the laboratory, answer it in part. The Alanya fishermen were not a five-hundred-year community. They were a hundred men who had been fighting each other in the early seventies and who built a working institution in a few years, out of a list and a lottery. Trust in that case came after the rules, not before, and that sequence is the possibility the shelf's cynical season had stopped believing in.

Chapter Nine: What a Hospital Holds in Common

I want to run the eight properties over something closer to home, and I will build the case rather than borrow one, so it is constructed, assembled from things that happen in every hospital I have worked in. A department shares an ultrasound machine. Six teams use it; it lives on a trolley; it is needed most between eight and ten in the morning, and by ten it has usually vanished into a side room with a probe missing and its battery flat. Complaints go to the manager, who sends an email saying the machine must be returned to the store after use, which is Hardin's coercion with no coercer, and it changes nothing, because nobody can see who took it and no consequence attaches to the taking.

Now read the principles over it. Who is in? Nobody has said, so the machine is also used by the outpatient clinic, a visiting fellow, and a radiographer from the next floor, and none of them know the rule because there is no group to belong to. Do the rules fit? The rule is return it to the store, which fails at eight in the morning when four teams need it inside the same hour; the rule that would fit is a rotation, the way the Alanya fishermen rotated spots. Who makes the rules? The manager did, alone, in an email; none of the six teams was asked, so none of them owns it. Who watches? Nobody; there is no sign-out sheet, so the team whose turn is next cannot see who has it, and that visibility was the free monitoring the huerta got from the farmer downstream. What happens when it is broken? Either nothing or a furious email to everyone, the opposite of graduated. Where do disputes go? To the same manager, weeks later. Does the outside allow it?
