The hospital would not object to six teams making their own arrangement, but no one has asked. And the layers: the machine is one of a dozen shared things in the department, each with the same problem, and there is no body that meets about any of them.

The fix that the book implies is not a better email. It is a group: the six teams named, meeting once, for half an hour, to agree a morning rotation, a sign-out board on the trolley, and a rule that the team who returns it flat charges it before their next turn. It is a commons institution, of the smallest possible kind, and it works where the email did not because the people who use the resource made the rule, can see who broke it, and can do something small about it by lunchtime. Most of what a manager governs is like the ultrasound machine, and most of it is being governed by email.

Chapter Ten: Verdict, Dose, and a Question

The verdict is that Governing the Commons is the most hopeful book on this shelf and the best argued, and that both properties come from the same source, which is that Ostrom made no claim she had not gone and checked. The reading prescription is the book itself, chapters three and five first, the cases and the failures, and the design principles chapter only after you have the cases in your head, because read alone the principles are a list and read after Törbel they are a pattern you have already seen. Then Hardin's essay, which takes twenty minutes and which you should read to find out what was actually in it. Then Agrawal, for the strongest friendly objection, and Cox and colleagues for the answer.

The dose is the reverse of the shelf's usual warning. The cynical canon is medicine in small quantities and poison as a worldview. Ostrom is safe at any dose, and the risk with her runs the other way: a reader can come away believing that every commons can be governed by its users, and the book's failed cases are there to prevent that. Read the failures twice.

The question to carry into next week is a small one. Name one thing your department holds in common that is being managed by email. The machine, the room, the on-call rota, the fridge, the shared drive. Then ask the first three of Ostrom's questions of it: who is in, does the rule fit the hour when it is needed, and did the people who use it have any part in making the rule. If the answer to the third is no, you have found the reason the email did not work, and you have also found the half-hour meeting that would.

Next time, the third antidote, and the first book on this shelf written by someone who ran a large organisation and thought it went rather well: Andy Grove's High Output Management, on the breakfast factory, the one-on-one, and what a manager's output actually is. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty (Hirschman): what to do when your institution declines
item.description: Albert Hirschman's 1970 book as the first of four antidotes to the shelf's cynical season – the Nigerian railway, the lazy monopoly, loyalty as a brake, the East German test that broke his own theory, and what a ward loses when its best nurses leave without a word.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: A Change of Plan, and a Question

Last time I promised Notes on Nationalism, and it is coming, but not yet. Shooting an Elephant was the darkest half hour this feed has produced, and it closed a month on the machinery of decline: Jackall's managers arranging blame, Davies's sinks, Whyte's organization man, Parkinson, Peter, Graeber's feudal retinues, Scott's high modernists levelling villages, Orwell's soft snow and his rifle. Read one after another, those books teach a lesson none of them intended, which is that nothing can be done, and that lesson is false. Every one of those authors got up in the morning and did something. So the next four episodes are the shelf's antidote season: four books about what a person can do inside an institution, on the assumption that the person is you, and the institution is one you cannot simply leave. The first is Albert Hirschman's Exit, Voice, and Loyalty, from nineteen seventy, and it begins with a question so plain that it took an economist of unusual character to ask it.

The question is this. Something you belong to, a firm, a clinic, a party, a church, a country, has started to get worse. Not collapsed; slipped. The product is a little shoddier, the meetings a little emptier, the waiting list a little longer. What do you do? Hirschman's answer is that there are two things you can do and only two. You can leave, which he calls exit. Or you can stay and complain, which he calls voice. Everything in the book follows from the observation that these two responses are not just different for you; they are different for the institution, because one of them carries information and the other one carries a customer out the door.

Chapter Two: The Man Who Asked

Hirschman is the kind of author who makes the biography compulsory, because the book is the biography with the names removed. He was born Otto Albert Hirschmann in Berlin in nineteen fifteen, left Germany at eighteen, a few weeks after Hitler came to power, studied in Paris and London and Trieste, fought for the Republic in Spain, and then, in nineteen forty, did the thing that his biographer Jeremy Adelman puts at the centre of the life. In Marseille he became the operations man for Varian Fry's rescue committee, the American who smuggled some two thousand refugees out of Vichy France, among them Chagall, Arendt, and Marc Bloch's manuscripts. Fry called him Beamish, for the grin. Hirschman forged documents, changed money on the black market, and walked people over the Pyrenees. When the Vichy police came for him he walked over the mountains himself.

Hold that man in mind, because he is the author of a book about leaving. He knew what exit costs and what it saves, in the only currency that counts, and he knew that voice inside a regime that has decided to kill you is a death sentence with extra steps. Then he spent the fifties as an economic adviser in Colombia, where he learned to distrust the grand plan, and wrote The Strategy of Economic Development, which argues that the way to develop a poor country is not to balance everything at once but to create imbalances that force the next step. He would go on to write The Passions and the Interests, on how commerce was once sold as a civilising force, and The Rhetoric of Reaction, which catalogues the three arguments every conservative uses against every reform: it will backfire, it will change nothing, it will endanger what we already have. That book is a machine for hearing your own excuses, and it belongs on this shelf on its own.

Exit, Voice, and Loyalty came in between, and the story of how it started is in the first chapter. In the sixties Hirschman was looking at the Nigerian railways, which were bad, and getting worse, in a country where they mattered, and he wanted to know why nobody was fixing them. The standard answer was inefficiency and corruption. His answer was trucks.

Chapter Three: The Railway and the Trucks

Here is the mechanism, run all the way through, because it is the book. The Nigerian railway carried freight, and it carried it badly. In most theories of the market, that is a self-correcting condition. Customers desert the bad supplier, who then either improves or dies; either way the problem is solved. Nigeria had a road haulage industry, so the customers deserted. Peanut shippers and cotton shippers moved their freight to lorries. And the railway did not improve and did not die. It got worse, and it went on getting worse, for years.

Hirschman's explanation begins with a question about who left. The customers who moved to the trucks first were the ones who cared most about delivery times, the ones who had been complaining loudest, the ones with the alternative and the motive to use it. Those were the railway's most useful customers, and their value had nothing to do with the freight charges; they were the ones who would have kicked. Once they were gone, the railway was left with the shippers who did not much mind, or could not move, and the pressure that might have driven a repair went out onto the road with the freight. The railway was a public enterprise, so it did not go bankrupt either; the state covered the deficit. Exit had drained the voice and the treasury had cancelled the death, and in that condition an organisation can decline indefinitely, with a kind of peace.

There is a refinement in the book that I think is its most practical page, and it concerns who leaves first. Hirschman distinguishes customers by how much they care about quality as against price. When a product deteriorates, the quality-sensitive customers, the ones he calls connoisseurs, feel it first and leave first, because for them the drop in quality is a large price rise. The price-sensitive customers barely register it. So the order of exit is fixed by the structure of the customers' preferences, and it is the worst possible order for the organisation: it loses its most discriminating members at the first sign of trouble and keeps the ones who cannot tell. The department losing its best registrars in the year the teaching went bad is not suffering bad luck. It is running Hirschman's sequence on schedule.

This is the argument's first turn, and I want to state it the way Hirschman does, because it is a claim against his own discipline. Economics had treated exit as the whole of the story. Competition works because people leave. Voice, the complaint, the letter, the delegation to the manager, the vote, was something political scientists talked about and economists treated as noise. Hirschman's claim is that these are two mechanisms of recovery, that they interact, and that in a large class of cases the presence of an easy exit destroys voice by draining off the people who would have used it. The competition that was supposed to discipline the railway had instead anaesthetised it.

He then generalises, and the generalisation is the part that most readers remember. Think of American public schools in a city where some parents can afford private ones. When the public school slips, the parents who see it first and care most are, disproportionately, the ones who can pay to leave. They leave. The school loses the very parents who would have turned up at the board meeting, and its decline proceeds with less resistance than before. Hirschman is careful here, more careful than the people who later quoted him: he does not say private schools are wrong, or that exit should be blocked. He says that an option which is good for each leaver can be bad for the institution and for everyone who stays, and that anyone designing the choice needs to know this.

He runs the same logic through politics, in a chapter that reads oddly in a season when the shelf has been so hard on parties. Anthony Downs had argued that in a two-party system both parties drift to the centre, because the voters at the extremes have nowhere else to go. Hirschman's reply is that a voter who cannot exit does not go quiet; he gets loud. The captive member of a party is the member most likely to use voice, since voice is all he has, and a party that takes its base for granted because the base cannot leave has misread the situation as thoroughly as the railway did. The prediction was made in nineteen seventy. Anyone who has watched a party's activists drag it away from the centre since then has watched the prediction come in, and this is one place where the book, rather than its critics, has aged well.

Chapter Four: The Monopolist Who Would Rather Be Left Alone

A second mechanism, and this one comes with a label I have never been able to forget. Hirschman's term for it is the lazy monopoly. The textbook monopolist is greedy, and squeezes the customer. Hirschman describes a different creature: the monopolist who is tired rather than greedy, who would rather have a quiet life than a large profit, and for whom a certain amount of exit is a relief. If the customers who leave are the fussy ones, the ones who write letters and demand to see someone, then their departure improves the day of everybody who works there. The organisation is not fighting exit. It is welcoming it, because exit is how it sheds its critics.

He gives examples from the sixties and I will give one from a hospital, constructed, but assembled from real parts. A department has a difficult senior nurse, the kind who reads the drug chart the doctor has just written and asks about the dose. She is right often enough to be a nuisance. She has been raising the same three issues at the staff meeting for two years: the missing night cover, the broken observation machine on bay four, the handover that takes place in a corridor. Nothing changes, because nothing has to; her complaints are absorbed, minuted, and filed. One day she takes a job at the private hospital across town, where the observation machines work. The department's official response is regret. Its actual response is relief. The meeting is shorter now. The drug charts are not read as closely, and it will be some months before anybody notices the dose that gets through. Hirschman's insight, and it is an insight about institutions rather than people, is that the department did not push her out. It simply made staying pointless and leaving easy, and the mechanism did the rest.

The shelf has met this before under other names. Davies's accountability sink, from episode two, is a structure that ensures the complaint can find nobody to land on. Hirschman gives you the flow that the sink is built to handle. Voice arrives, is absorbed, achieves nothing, and the person who raised it does the arithmetic and exits, and the sink's designers count the exit as a problem solved. Whyte's organization man, from the sixth episode, is the opposite figure: the man who has decided never to exit and has, over the years, lost the capacity for voice too, so that loyalty in him has become mere presence. Hirschman is the writer who explains why both figures are stable.

Chapter Five: Loyalty, the Brake

Which brings the book to its third term, and the term Hirschman himself was least sure of. If exit drains voice, then something has to hold people in place long enough for voice to be tried, and that something he calls loyalty. He does not mean sentiment. He means whatever it is that makes a person delay exit, that makes them say, this place has been good and I will give it another year, or, if I go, who will say this. Loyalty in his sense is a brake on exit and therefore a subsidy to voice. It buys the organisation time in which the complaint can work.

He is clear that loyalty can be manufactured, and that the manufacturers are not always friends of the institution. High entry costs, initiation rituals, the years of training that a profession demands, all raise the price of exit and so all increase the reliance on voice. A medical training is, among other things, a loyalty device: it is so expensive to become a doctor that most doctors stay, and complain, rather than leave. Whether that is good depends entirely on whether the complaints are heard. Hirschman also flags the perverse case: the member so loyal that they never leave and never speak, who has converted the brake into a parking brake. That is Whyte's man again, and it is the loyalty of the party member who stays through the purges. Loyalty is only a virtue in his scheme when it is the kind that ends in voice, and, if voice fails, in exit. The threat of exit, kept credible, is what gives voice its force. A complaint from someone who will never leave is a complaint the institution can afford to ignore.

Here the clinician's lens has something to add. Medicine's culture teaches loyalty of the wrong kind. The unwritten rules, do not go over your consultant's head, do not embarrass the department, do not put it in writing, are all devices for suppressing voice while keeping the member. The result is the department where the problems are known to everyone and said by no one, where the exits happen silently and are read as personal decisions, and where the first outsider to look sees a pattern the insiders could not. Hirschman would say such a department has arranged its incentives to receive neither signal. It has made voice futile and exit quiet, and it has done so while congratulating itself on staff retention.

Chapter Six: When Exit Became Policy

The book did not stay on the shelf, and the place it went is one a clinician should know about, because it went into the hospital. In the two thousands the British government, advised by the economist Julian Le Grand, rebuilt the National Health Service around patient choice: publish the hospitals' results, let patients choose where to be treated, let the money follow the patient. Le Grand's book on the reform, The Other Invisible Hand, from two thousand and seven, argues the case in Hirschman's vocabulary. Voice, he says, had been tried for fifty years in the health service, through complaints procedures and community health councils and the ballot box, and it had failed, because voice favours the articulate. The middle-class patient who knows how to write a letter gets heard; the patient who does not, does not. Exit, by contrast, is available to anyone who can get on a bus. Give every patient the power to leave, and the hospitals will have to improve for everyone, since they cannot tell in advance which patient will walk.

That is a real argument and a fair use of the book, and the shelf owes it the steelman. It is also, on Hirschman's own account, incomplete, and he would have said so. First, the exit has to be real. A patient with a broken hip does not shop; a patient in a rural district has one hospital; and a patient whose general practitioner makes the referral is exercising the doctor's exit, not their own. Second, and this is the railway again, the exits that happen will be the connoisseurs', the informed patients with cars, and their departure will lower the pressure on the hospital they left unless the money that follows them is large enough to hurt, and in a public system it rarely is. Third, choice was introduced alongside a deliberate effort to keep hospitals open, because closing one is a political catastrophe, and that combination, easy exit with no death, is the Nigerian railway's exact configuration. The evidence since has been argued over for two decades, with studies from Zack Cooper and colleagues at the London School of Economics finding modest gains in mortality and management quality in areas with more competition, and others finding little. What I take from it is smaller than either side's claim: Hirschman gives you the checklist for whether an exit-based reform can work, and the checklist was not run.

There is one more figure in the book that the health-service story needs, and it is the boycott. Hirschman notes that a boycott is exit used as voice: the customers leave, but they leave loudly, with a demand attached, and they announce the terms on which they will return. It is the one form in which the two mechanisms combine on purpose, and it foreshadows the East German case he would not understand for another twenty years. A profession that wanted to change a hospital could learn from it. The junior doctors who leave one at a time, each with a personal reason, are Hirschman's silent exiters, and their departures teach the hospital nothing. The same doctors, leaving together with a stated reason and a stated condition of return, are a boycott, and a boycott is the only exit an institution is built to hear.

Chapter Seven: The Case Against, and the Case He Made Against Himself

Now the objections, and there are serious ones. The first came in nineteen seventy-four from the political theorist Brian Barry, in a long review that admirers of the book still have to answer. Barry's complaint was about the structure. Hirschman presents exit and voice as if they were one choice, and Barry pointed out that they are two. First comes the choice to stay or go. Then, having stayed, a second choice: speak or keep quiet. Silence is an option, and a common one, and the book's neat pairing hides it. Barry also went after loyalty, and the phrase he used has stuck: loyalty, he said, was an equation filler, a term Hirschman brought in to make the model come out, defined mostly by what it needed to do. Keith Dowding and colleagues, reviewing the whole literature in two thousand, reached a similar place from a gentler direction: the schema is more complicated than it looks, the empirical basis of loyalty is thin, and to test the theory you have to pull its parts apart in ways the book never did. There is a family of formal models since, William Clark and Matt Golder's among them, that rebuild the argument as a game and find that some of Hirschman's results hold and some depend on assumptions he did not state.

I think Barry is right about the structure and mostly right about loyalty, and I think it costs the book less than it should. The two-stage version is better, and it is the version a clinician needs, because silence is the modal response in any hospital, and a theory that has no box for it is a theory that cannot see the ward. Loyalty as Hirschman used it is underdefined, and its best defence is that he said so: he calls the chapter a first try and ends the book with a list of the cases he could not handle.

Then there is the objection that Hirschman made against himself, and it is the reason I trust him. In nineteen eighty-nine East Germans started leaving through Hungary, and then through Czechoslovakia, by the tens of thousands. On the theory, that exit should have drained the voice: the people who could leave would leave, the regime would be left with the compliant, and the Leipzig demonstrations should have fizzled. The opposite happened. The exodus and the demonstrations grew together, each feeding the other, until the state fell. Hirschman, then in his late seventies, wrote a paper about it in nineteen ninety-three, and its argument is that his own book had been wrong about the relation of the two mechanisms. He had treated them as substitutes, one draining the other. In East Germany they were complements: the exit proved that the regime could not hold its people, and the demonstration proved that the people who stayed were not consenting, and each message made the other credible. He described the paper as the correction of an error of his own, with a clarity that few authors manage about their best-known work. A theory whose author can be seen revising it against evidence has a property the shelf has been looking for all season, and most of the cynical canon does not have it.

Chapter Eight: What This Gives a Manager

The four books in this antidote season are for the person inside, and Hirschman's is the most useful of the four for the person who is not yet in charge, because it is a theory of what your options are and how the institution reads them. But it also says something to the person who is in charge, and I want to draw it out, because it is not in the book as a chapter and it is the reason a manager should read it.

If you run anything, Hirschman tells you where your information comes from, and it is not from the people who are happy. It comes from the people who complain and stay, and it comes, in a form you have to learn to read, from the people who leave. The manager's first job on this theory is to make voice cheap. That means answering it, visibly, even when the answer is no, because a complaint that is minuted and filed teaches the complainant that the mechanism is dead, and the next person will not bother. It means protecting the people who use voice, since the nurse who reads the drug chart is the department's early warning system and every manager who has ever found her tiresome has confused the sensor with the noise. And it means reading exits as data: when someone leaves, the useful question is what they knew, and whether the department has now lost the last person who would have said it.

Let me run that through one case, constructed again, so that the abstraction has a shape. A clinical director inherits a department with a turnover problem: five junior doctors gone in eighteen months, each departure explained at the time by a personal reason, a partner's job, a fellowship, a move home. She does the thing Hirschman implies and nobody does, which is to go back through the previous two years of staff meeting minutes and find what each of the five had raised. Four of them had brought up the same item: the weekend handover, at which the departing team briefed the arriving one in a room where the phone rang continuously and the list was on a whiteboard that had been half-erased. Each had raised it once, been told it was on the list, and not raised it again. None of them mentioned it when they resigned. That last fact is the one to hold onto. By the time a person exits, they have usually stopped using voice, and the exit interview asks the question a year too late. The director moves the handover to a room with a door, prints the list, and unplugs the phone for twenty minutes. She cannot prove that this is why the next eighteen months lose one junior instead of five. She can say that the two years of minutes had contained the answer, in the voices of the people who then left, and that nobody had been reading them as a message because each one, alone, had looked like a comment.

The second job is to keep exit visible. An organisation that can watch its exits and ask what they mean is one that can still learn. Hirschman's railway could not, because the state paid the deficit and the exits were just numbers on a freight sheet. A department that counts staff turnover as a cost line rather than a message has built the same railway. The manager who reads Hirschman and does one thing should do this: for every departure in the next year, find out what the person had been saying for the previous two, and whether anybody had answered.

There is a third thing, and it is about the manager's own exit. Hirschman's argument gives the person in charge a reason to keep their own exit credible. A manager who cannot leave, who has staked the mortgage and the identity on the job, is a manager whose voice upward has no force, because the people above know they will stay through anything. The shelf's cynical books were full of such people, and Jackall's managers, from the first episode, were their purest form. The reading of Hirschman that helps is that loyalty is a brake you apply for a purpose, and a brake that is never released is a wheel that no longer turns.

Chapter Nine: Verdict, Dose, and a Question

The verdict is that this is a short book, a hundred and sixty pages, which every person who belongs to anything should read, and that it should be read with Barry's correction in hand and Hirschman's East German paper afterwards. Its predictions fail often enough that you should not use it to predict. Its categories are right so consistently that you will not be able to stop using them to see. The reading prescription is the book, in one sitting; Barry's review if you can find it, which is in the British Journal of Political Science for nineteen seventy-four; and the nineteen ninety-three paper, which is in World Politics and is the best thing on the list.

The dose is different from the cynical books, and I want to be explicit about why. Jackall and Davies are diagnostic in small amounts and poisonous as an identity, because a person who has fully absorbed them stops acting. Hirschman is the reverse. He is a theory of action, and its side effect is a slightly too neat belief that your options are always two. Take him in full doses, and correct for the neatness with Barry.

The question to take back to work is in two parts, and you should ask it about the place you work rather than about yourself. First: who has left in the last year, and what had they been saying? Write the names down; there will be fewer than you think, and the pattern will be clearer than you expect. Second: who is still there, saying the same thing for two years, heard by nobody? That person is your railway's last complaining customer. Find out what it would cost to answer them, and then compare it to what it will cost when they take the job across town.

Next time, the second antidote, and the one that answers a question this shelf's whole cynical season has been assuming has no answer: whether people can run a shared resource without a boss and without a market. Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons, on the Swiss villagers, the Spanish water courts, and the Nobel Prize that went to the woman who went and looked. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Orwell, Shooting an Elephant: a man captured by his audience
item.description: Orwell's 1936 Burma essay read as the cleanest specimen ever written of an actor captured by his own audience, paired with the earlier 'A Hanging' and set against the dispute over whether either one really happened.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Man Who Has to Do Something

Here is a scene I have watched from the foot of the bed, and I should say up front that the patient in it is built from several real ones and is not any single case file. A man is dying of something that cannot be fixed, slowly enough that everyone in the room knows it, and his daughter, who flew in that morning, asks the covering physician what more can be done. The truthful answer is nothing that will change the outcome. The physician orders a scan anyway. Not because the scan will tell him anything he does not already know, but because a room full of frightened people is watching him, and the only visible difference between a doctor who has given up and a doctor who is still fighting is whether an order gets written, and he cannot stand to look like the first kind. The scan changes nothing about the man in the bed. It changes everything about how the physician feels leaving the room, and that second fact, not the first, is what actually decided the order.

I want you to hold that scene loosely for the length of this episode, because the essay we are reading today is the cleanest specimen anyone has ever written of the mechanism inside it: a man with formal authority over a situation who no longer has any actual say in what he does, because a crowd he cannot ignore has already decided what the authority is for. The essay is called Shooting an Elephant. It runs to about three thousand words, it was written by a twenty-three-year-old colonial policeman remembering something that may or may not have happened exactly as he tells it, and its animal is real in a way the scan is not: something living dies at the end of it, slowly, in public, for a reason its killer states as plainly as any sentence in the English language, which is that he could not bear to be laughed at.

Chapter Two: Five Years in a Uniform He Came to Hate

Eric Blair was nineteen when he sailed for Burma in 1922, a King's Scholar from Eton who had not gone on to Oxford or Cambridge because his family could not easily afford it, and who joined the Indian Imperial Police instead because it was a career that took boys straight from school. He spent five years in it, most of them in small Burmese towns doing the unglamorous work of colonial administration: petty courts, tax disputes, and the police stations where information got extracted from suspects by methods he later wrote about with disgust. By the biographer Michael Shelden's dating, he held his most senior post, sub-divisional officer at Moulmein in the country's south, from April to December of 1926, in sole charge of policing a district of some hundred thousand people at an age when most of his Eton contemporaries were finishing university. The critic Christopher Hitchens, reading the Burma years for his book Why Orwell Matters, notes that Blair worried even at the time that the job was turning him into something between a sadist and an automaton, a man trained to produce the correct response to a situation whether or not he believed in it. Blair resigned in 1927, came home, and told his family he never wanted to hear the word Burma again. He did not keep that promise. His first novel, Burmese Days, published in 1934, is a direct settling of accounts with the colonial society he had lived inside, savage enough about his former colleagues that his publisher's lawyers made him change names before they would print it. The journalist Emma Larkin, who spent years retracing his postings for her book Finding George Orwell in Burma, calls Burmese Days, Animal Farm, and Nineteen Eighty-Four an unintended trilogy: the country where he first watched what unaccountable power does to the people who hold it, and the two books where he later worked out what he had seen.

Two essays came directly out of those five years, five and ten years apart, and this episode is going to read them together. The later one, from 1936, is the elephant. The earlier one, written in 1931 for a small magazine called the Adelphi, is called A Hanging, and it belongs in the same frame for a reason that will only become clear once we have both scenes in front of us: it shows the same institution doing the same kind of damage to the same young officer, but with no crowd in it at all. Keep it in reserve. We will need the contrast.

Chapter Three: A Dead Man and a Peaceful Elephant

The elephant essay opens with a sentence that tells you, in one line, everything about the position the whole piece will examine. In Moulmein, Orwell writes, he was hated by large numbers of people, the only time in his life he had been important enough for that to happen to him. Importance and hatred arrive together, and neither is separable from the uniform.

The plot is simple and he tells it fast. A tame elephant kept by a timber company has broken its chain while in what Orwell calls a state of must, the periodic surge of aggression bull elephants go through and normally sit out chained up until it passes, and has spent the morning wrecking a bazaar stall and, by the time Orwell is sent for, has trampled a Burmese laborer to death. The condition is temporary and well understood by anyone who works with elephants for a living, which is part of what makes the rest of the essay's decision so exposed: the animal is not permanently dangerous, only dangerous on a schedule its owner already knows how to wait out. He describes the body once, in a single unsparing paragraph: the man on his belly with his arms flung wide, his face pressed into the mud, his teeth bared in what Orwell calls an expression of unendurable agony. Then he sends for an elephant rifle, more as a precaution than a plan, and rides out to find the animal.

He finds it grazing peacefully in a paddy field, its dangerous fit apparently over, doing nothing more alarming than an elephant tearing up grass with its trunk and swishing it against its knees to clean the dirt off, and he tells us, in a sentence that matters more than anything else in the first half of the essay, that he had made up his mind not to shoot it: he did not in the least want to. A working elephant is valuable, worth, he notes later, more alive than dead by a factor most Europeans in the room would have found obvious, and killing one for a crime already committed and apparently over struck him as something between a waste and a crime of its own. He meant to watch it a while longer, satisfy himself it had calmed down, and walk home.

That is the man who arrives at the paddy field. He is not there yet, on the page, as the man who kills the elephant. Something happens between that sentence and the one three pages later where the trigger gets pulled, and the thing that happens is the actual subject of the essay, not the elephant and not even, in the end, the empire. It is an audience.

Chapter Four: Two Thousand Wills and One Rifle

Word had traveled ahead of him. By the time Orwell reaches the field, a crowd has assembled behind him along the road, growing as he walks, until he estimates it at two thousand people at the least, all watching him the way, he says, they would watch a conjurer about to perform a trick. They have brought nothing to do but watch. He is the only person present with a rifle, and the rifle is the only reason two thousand people are standing in a paddy field on a hot afternoon instead of doing whatever they would otherwise be doing. They want to see the elephant shot, and they have no other use for him.

He describes what happens in his own mind with a precision that should embarrass anyone who has ever claimed authority he did not actually hold. He looks at the elephant, sees a beast that has done its damage and stopped, and privately concludes there is no case for shooting it. And then he looks at the crowd behind him, and understands, in his own words, the hollowness and the futility of the white man's rule in the East. The empire he represents exists, in that field, as a story the crowd has been told about what a sahib does, and the story requires him to act. If he orders the elephant left alone, two thousand Burmans will watch a white man who was afraid, and word of that will travel faster and further than any court record, and the entire machinery of colonial authority, which runs on nothing sturdier than the belief that the men who hold guns will use them, will have lost a little of its charge in front of the one audience it can least afford to lose it in front of.

He supplies his own image for what this makes him, and it is worth hearing exactly as he wrote it. A white man who turns tyrant, he says, destroys his own freedom in the act: he becomes a hollow, posing dummy, the conventionalized figure of a sahib, obliged to spend his life trying to impress the natives, doing in every crisis what the natives expect of him. He wears a mask, in his own phrase, and his face grows to fit it. The natives are not, on this account, the ones without power in the field. They have the only vote that counts, because they have decided in advance what the man with the gun is for, and he has no way to refuse the role without becoming, in front of the one audience that matters to his authority, a joke instead of a ruler. Orwell puts it more bluntly than the theory needs: he was, he writes, only an absurd puppet pushed to and fro by the will of the yellow faces behind him.

That is a strange sentence for a man wearing a colonial uniform to have written. The entire administrative apparatus behind him, the courts, the garrison, the telegraph line back to Rangoon, exists to make the claim that the sahib commands and the subject obeys, and Orwell is standing in a paddy field reporting the opposite chain of command with his own name attached to it. He does not say the system is unjust and leave it there, which would have cost him nothing. He says the system had already stripped him of the one thing a ruler is supposed to keep, his own judgment about what to do with force, and replaced it with a performance scheduled entirely by the people he was sent there to rule. The mask is not a disguise he could take off at the end of the shift. It had already grown into the only face available to him in public, and a face that has grown to fit a mask does not come back off clean.

Look closely at what has actually happened to the decision. Nobody has ordered him to shoot. There is no superior officer present, no regulation requiring it, nothing but two thousand people standing still. And that is a stronger instrument than any order could have been, because an order can be disobeyed and blamed on the man who gave it, while an audience's expectation cannot be disobeyed without the actor himself absorbing the whole cost of the refusal. The frightened family at the foot of the bed in this episode's opening scene is not a court either. It has no authority over the physician's license, no power to file a complaint that would stick. It only has to stand there.

Chapter Five: What Killing It Actually Looked Like

He fires from about twenty-five yards, and the essay does not spare the reader the mechanics of what an elephant rifle actually does to an animal that size when the man holding it has never shot one before. At the first shot the animal sags at the knees, its mouth falling open, and Orwell reads in that single change of posture what he calls a mysterious, terrible change come over it, as though the huge shot had paralyzed it without knocking it down. It does not die. He fires again, and it seems to gather itself and stand a little taller before it begins, at last, to fall, and he describes the fall in a sentence that has outlived the rest of the essay in most readers' memory: the animal's trunk reaching skyward as it trumpets, for the first and only time in the whole account, before it comes down with a crash that shakes the ground he is standing on. Even that is not the end. It kneels, rights itself, kneels again, and lies on its side breathing in long, rhythmic, rattling gasps, its great flank rising and falling, for a stretch of time Orwell puts at half an hour before he finally leaves, unable to watch any longer, while men arrive with knives to strip the carcass before it has finished dying.

What follows the death is where the essay stops being a story about an animal and turns into a piece of testimony against its own narrator, and the turn is total. The Europeans who hear about it afterward split along a generational line: the older men agree he was right, the younger men call it a shame to destroy a valuable working elephant over the death of a single hired laborer, whose life several of them rate, out loud, as worth less than the animal's market price. And then Orwell delivers the line the whole essay has been building toward, and delivers it without a shred of the cover a lesser writer would have reached for. He tells us he was glad the laborer had been killed, because the man's death put him legally in the right and gave him, in his own phrase, a sufficient pretext for shooting the elephant. The dead man is useful to him. He says so.

Ten years after writing that sentence, Orwell would publish an essay this shelf has already read, arguing that a political language exists mainly to let people describe what they have done without having to feel it, that phrases like transfer of population let a man say a true thing without the image attached to it. Read this essay against that one and the relationship reverses in an interesting way. Shooting an Elephant contains no euphemism at all. Glad that the coolie had been killed is not a passive construction with the actor scrubbed out. It has a subject, a verb, and an object, and the subject is the man writing the sentence, confessing to being pleased about a death because the death served him. A decade before he wrote the rule about the checkable sentence, he had already written the exhibit: the plainest possible English, deployed not to protect himself but to convict himself, closing on the admission that he pulled the trigger, as he puts it, solely to avoid looking a fool.

Chapter Six: The One Without a Crowd

Now bring in A Hanging, written five years earlier, because it runs the same experiment with the audience removed, and the result should worry you more, not less.

There is no crowd in A Hanging. There are six or seven officials: Orwell, the superintendent, some Indian warders, and a condemned man being walked the last few yards to a gallows inside a prison yard where nobody outside the service will ever hear what happened. And yet the same paralysis occurs, produced this time not by two thousand watching faces but by a schedule. The hanging happens because eight o'clock has arrived and the appointed procedure runs on its own momentum, no single person in the yard actually choosing, moment to moment, that a man should die; the clock and the rulebook have already chosen, and everyone present is simply discharging a function that was decided somewhere else, by someone none of them can name.

The condemned man himself is a small, unremarkable figure, a Hindu with a shaved head and a moustache Orwell describes as absurdly large for so slight a body, the kind of detail a man notices when he is looking anywhere except at what is about to happen. Orwell gives the essay one image that does the same work as the elephant's trumpet: on the walk to the gallows, the prisoner steps neatly aside to avoid a puddle in the path, a wholly unnecessary courtesy from a man who will be dead in two minutes, and it is that detail, not the fact of the execution itself, that makes Orwell write the essay's real sentence: that he had never before realized what it means to destroy a healthy, conscious man who is still, in that instant, taking care about his shoes. A dog gets loose in the yard moments later and bounds straight for the prisoner to lick his face before the warders can catch it, an animal that has not been told what is supposed to happen and behaves accordingly, and Orwell notices that everyone present treats the dog's confusion as the awkward moment, not the hanging.

Once the noose is on, the prisoner begins calling out a single word, over and over, in a high, steady rhythm Orwell compares to the tolling of a bell rather than a cry for help, and the cotton bag the hangman lowers over his face muffles the sound without stopping it. Nobody present decides to end it. A lever is pulled at a signal, there is one clanking noise, and then, in Orwell's own description, dead silence. The mechanism, not any person in the yard, is what supplies the answer to a sound that had started to feel like it might go on. After it is over, the officials share a drink and jokes flow with a speed Orwell finds sinister for how easy it is: the superintendent pokes the body with his stick and pronounces it, with visible relief, all right, and men who spent the last ten minutes performing a killing spend the next ten laughing about a Burmese officer's poor grasp of English. The essay's last line places the corpse at a specific, ordinary distance from the drinking party: a hundred yards away.

Put the two essays side by side and you get a fuller map of the trap than either supplies alone. The elephant shows an audience forcing an actor to perform a decision he has already made against; the hanging shows a procedure eliminating the decision altogether, so thoroughly that the men executing it can laugh within minutes because none of them, individually, feels he did anything. One captures the actor by making him visible. The other releases him by making the act invisible, distributed across a schedule and a rulebook until no single hand seems to have held the rope. Both end with the person meant to be in charge having exercised no judgment whatsoever, and both were written by the same twenty-something who spent five years discovering that the uniform he wore did not put him in command of anything, least of all himself.

Chapter Seven: Whose Freedom the Tyrant Destroys

Give the essay its steelman before we turn on it, because there is a real case that this is one of the two or three most honest pieces of writing to come out of the whole colonial encounter, for the plain reason that it refuses the exculpation available to almost every officer who has ever done something he knew was wrong under pressure from below. A weaker writer tells this story as an unfortunate incident forced on him by circumstance and stops there. Orwell tells it as an incident that revealed circumstance to be the whole of colonial authority, that the sahib has no reserve of private judgment behind the public performance, because the empire had built him, deliberately, to have none. That is a claim about institutions generally, not only empires, and this shelf has been circling it since its first episode.

Put it next to Whyte's organization man from several episodes back, and the comparison sharpens rather than blurs the difference. Whyte's man surrendered his interior to the group and experienced the surrender as belonging; he believed the Social Ethic he was living by, and the belief is what made the surrender bearable. Orwell believes nothing of the kind. He tells us flatly, elsewhere in his Burma writing, that he already considered imperialism an evil thing and secretly sided with the Burmese against the government he served, hating the job, in his own words, more bitterly than he could easily explain, and shoots the elephant anyway, with his contempt for the whole system fully intact the entire time. That is the harder case, and the more useful one: obedience that survives disbelief, produced not by conviction but by the plain cost of visible refusal. A man who believes in the group, like Whyte's, needs no explanation for why he conforms. A man who despises the group and conforms anyway is the one who actually tells you how much force the performance carries on its own, stripped of every ideological reason someone might otherwise credit for the outcome.

Jackall's managers in Moral Mazes learn to look up and look around, reading a boss's face for what he wants; Orwell's predicament runs the geometry in reverse, an officer nominally on top reading the faces of two thousand people nominally beneath him, and finding that the direction authority runs and the direction power actually flows are not the same question at all. Burnham's admirers, several episodes ago, mistook whoever currently held the whip for the person actually deciding anything; Orwell, standing in the field with the whip in his own hands, tells you what it feels like from the other end of that mistake, which is that holding the whip decided nothing about who was in charge of the afternoon. The three frames converge on the same finding stated three different ways: watch where the eyes point, not where the badge sits, and you will generally find the real chain of command running the opposite direction from the org chart.

Chapter Eight: The Case Against, in Two Parts

The first count against the essay is not about its argument at all. It is about whether it happened.

Orwell's biographer Bernard Crick went looking for an official record of a colonial officer destroying a valuable timber elephant and found none, which he considered a genuine problem, since the loss of company property of that scale in British Burma would normally have generated paperwork and did not. The scholar Peter Davison, who edited Orwell's complete works, turned up two pieces of circumstantial evidence pulling in different directions. One is an interview with George Stuart, a contemporary of Orwell's in the Burma police, who recalled that Orwell was transferred from Moulmein to a quiet post at Katha in Upper Burma not long after the shooting, which Stuart read as a quiet reprimand for the same unauthorized destruction of property the essay describes. The other is a news item Davison found in the Rangoon Gazette of March 1926, reporting that a Major E. C. Kenny had shot an elephant in strikingly similar circumstances, which raises the possibility that Orwell, writing the essay a full decade later and from memory in London, folded another man's incident into his own or built the scene from a story he had heard secondhand and had never personally lived through the way the first-person voice insists he did.

Does that possibility matter to anything this episode has argued so far? Only partly, and the part that survives deserves a plain statement. If the mechanism the essay describes, an actor's judgment overridden by an audience with no formal authority over him, is true of colonial administration generally, which the historical record of the period supports independent of this one elephant, then the essay's core claim does not depend on this specific afternoon having occurred exactly as told. What does depend on it is the essay's authority as testimony, its claim to be reporting rather than composing, and a reader who cares about that distinction should hold the uncertainty rather than resolve it either way. Orwell wrote it as memory. The record cannot confirm memory and cannot quite convict it either.

The second count is sharper because it survives even if every fact in the essay is exactly true, and it comes from the literary scholar Pavan Kumar Malreddy, who has argued that Orwell's Burma writing runs two currents at once that the essay never quite separates: a shame at the empire's cruelty that is real, and a guilt about his own complicity that keeps recentering the story on the guilty man's feelings rather than the people the empire actually harmed. Look again at how the crowd is drawn. They are two thousand watching faces, an undifferentiated pressure with a single collective will, described at one point simply as yellow faces behind him, never once given a name, a sentence, or a reason of their own beyond the generic desire to see something killed. Orwell even hands the critique a piece of evidence himself, in a throwaway line about how a rumor always sounds clear at a distance and grows vaguer the nearer you get to it, which he offers as a fact about the East, full stop, the same confident generalization about an entire region's habits of mind that a writer who had truly escaped the colonial way of seeing would have caught himself making. The essay indicts the empire and, in the same paragraph, occasionally still narrates like one of its officers.

Malreddy's argument is not that this cancels the essay's honesty. It is that the honesty has a blind spot exactly where you would expect a colonial officer's honesty to have one, which is in his own vision, and that the essay is more valuable for what it can show us about that blind spot than it would be if we mistook it for a view from outside the empire altogether. Weigh what that does to the essay's most quoted line, the one about the tyrant destroying his own freedom. Read the way Malreddy reads it, the sentence is true and also a little convenient, because it lets a man who has just killed something make the story's central casualty his own liberty rather than the laborer already dead in the mud two pages earlier, or the elephant taking half an hour to stop breathing. The essay never forgets the coolie. It does, however, spend far more of its sentences on what the killing cost the killer than on what it cost anyone else, and a critic reading for whose interior life the prose actually dwells inside will find the answer is the Englishman's, every time.

Chapter Nine: Verdict, Dose, and the Question for Monday

Read it whole. It takes fifteen minutes, it is free everywhere online, and no summary, including this one, can substitute for watching the sentence structure carry the argument on its own, plain declarative clauses stacking up toward a confession the writer never once tries to soften. Read A Hanging alongside it in the same sitting, because the pairing is where the real instruction lives: the elephant essay hands you an actor captured by an audience he cannot walk away from, while the hanging gives you one relieved of having to be an actor at all, and between the two of them you get most of the ways an institution can take a decision away from the person nominally making it.

Take the uncertainty about whether it happened as it is told, not as a reason to discount the essay but as a live question you carry alongside it, the way you would carry a diagnosis made from a single unreplicated observation.

The dose here is diagnostic, and the instrument is a habit of paying attention to your own audience, not your own conscience. This week, catch yourself doing something, ordering the scan, sending the reassuring email, approving the request you have doubts about, and before you reach for the clinical or the administrative reason, ask a plainer one first: if nobody were going to see me not do this, would I still do it? If the answer changes depending on who is in the doorway, you have found your own paddy field, and the two thousand people in it are usually closer to three: whoever is actually watching, whoever you imagine will hear about it afterward, and the version of yourself you have to face in the mirror having failed to look decisive. Orwell's discovery was that only one of those three audiences has any real stake in the outcome, and it is never the one that gets obeyed.

The question to carry past Monday is the one the essay leaves you holding rather than answering: what is the elephant in your own institution, the animal that has already stopped being dangerous, that you are nonetheless about to shoot because a crowd assembled before you had time to think, and what would it cost you, specifically, today, to lower the rifle and walk home instead.

Next time, the shelf stays with Orwell for an essay about a habit of mind rather than a single afternoon: Notes on Nationalism, on the transferred loyalties that let an otherwise intelligent person classify whole populations like insects and refuse to see what is in front of him. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Orwell, Politics and the English Language: the six rules and the linguists against them
item.description: Orwell's 1946 essay read against the linguists who think it is nonsense – the six rules and their failures, the passive-voice count that embarrasses him, and the case that the mechanism is true even though the essay is bad.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: Two Sentences About the Same Thing

Here is a sentence from a clinical note, and I have changed nothing about it except the details that would identify anyone; the shape is one I have read a thousand times. The patient was found to have deteriorated overnight and appropriate measures were instituted. Now here is what happened. Nobody checked on him between midnight and six. At six the nurse found him grey and breathing at thirty a minute, and the registrar was called, and the registrar started oxygen and antibiotics and asked why nobody had called earlier. The first sentence is not false. Every word in it is defensible. It is also constructed so that nothing in it can be checked, because it has no nurse, no registrar, no six hours, and no question at the end, and the person who wrote it may not have been lying at all. He may simply have been writing the way the notes are written, in the register that was available to him, and the register did the concealing on his behalf.

That gap, between a sentence that is true and a sentence that can be checked, is the subject of the essay this episode is about, and you should have the subject in front of you before the essay arrives, because the essay is famous for something else. It is famous for six rules about style. The rules are the least defensible thing in it, and the linguists have spent forty years saying so, with numbers. What is underneath the rules is a claim about how language protects the people who use it from what they are saying, and that claim is not about style, and it has survived every objection that has been made to the rules. The plan for this episode is to take the objections seriously enough to concede the essay, and then show why the mechanism does not go down with it.

Chapter Two: An Essay Written in a Hurry by a Man Who Knew

Politics and the English Language was published in Horizon in April nineteen forty-six, four episodes ago in this shelf's chronology and a month before the essay on Burnham. Orwell was writing at the rate of a man who knew his time, and the two essays are twins: one about a mind corrupted by power, the other about a language corrupted by the need to defend it. He had reasons of his own to be interested. He had spent two years of the war at the BBC's Eastern Service, producing propaganda for India, and had come away with an insider's knowledge of what it feels like to write sentences whose purpose is to be broadcast rather than believed. He had also spent a decade reading the political pamphlets of the left, and he was the only prominent English socialist of his generation who wrote about the left's prose as if it were evidence.

The essay's structure is simple. He puts five specimens of bad contemporary writing on the table, a professor, a scientist, a psychologist, a Communist pamphlet, and a letter to Tribune, and he reads them the way this series tries to read everything, for the tells. Then he names four habits that the specimens share. Dying metaphors, figures of speech used so often that they no longer call up an image and are used only because they save the writer inventing a phrase. Operators, or verbal false limbs, the padding that replaces a simple verb with a phrase: render inoperative, militate against, make contact with, be subjected to, give rise to. Pretentious diction, the Latin and Greek words that dress a plain statement in a lab coat: phenomenon, element, objective, categorical, eliminate, liquidate. And meaningless words, the ones that in political and literary use have no agreed referent at all, so that a statement made with them cannot be contradicted: democracy, freedom, justice, realistic, and in criticism, living, vital, human.

Then the demonstration, the part of the essay that is still funny. He takes a verse of Ecclesiastes, the one about the race not being to the swift nor the battle to the strong, and translates it into the prose of the specimens: objective consideration of contemporary phenomena compels the conclusion that success or failure in competitive activities exhibits no tendency to be commensurate with innate capacity. The joke is precise. The translation is longer, has more syllables, contains not a single concrete image, and says less, and it is the kind of sentence that would be accepted without comment in any committee paper in the country. And his image for what has happened is the one line of the essay I would keep if I could keep one: a mass of Latin words falls upon the facts like soft snow, blurring the outlines and covering up all the details.

Chapter Three: The Rules, and What the Linguists Did to Them

The six rules come near the end, and they are what the essay has become in the culture, printed on the walls of newsrooms and copied into every style guide since. No figure of speech you are used to seeing in print. No long word where a short one will do. Any word that can be cut, cut. The active in preference to the passive. No foreign phrase, scientific term, or jargon where an everyday English word exists. And break any of these sooner than say anything outright barbarous.

The case against the rules is the best-documented case against anything on this shelf, because linguists count, and the counting was done by Geoffrey Pullum, co-author of the Cambridge Grammar of the English Language and for twenty years the most persistent critic of usage advice in the English-speaking world. Take rule four, the passive. Pullum went through the essay itself and counted the passive constructions against the transitive verbs, using the strict grammatical definition rather than the loose one style guides use. Roughly a quarter of Orwell's transitive verbs in the essay are passive. The rate in ordinary published prose, in the corpora linguists use to measure such things, is closer to one in six. Orwell used the passive more than the average writer, in the essay in which he told everyone else to stop. And Pullum's broader finding, from years of these counts, is that the pattern is general: the writers most exercised about the passive use it more than the rest of us, E. B. White included, because what they object to is the idea of it rather than the thing, and could not identify the thing in their own sentences if asked.

Take rule one. Pullum's objection, in a piece he called Elimination of the Fittest, is that banning every figure of speech a reader has seen before is a rule against the language. The familiar metaphors are the ones that worked; that is why you keep seeing them. Follow the rule to its limit and you strip out the most successful phrases first, then the next most successful, until what remains is either invented that morning or barbarous, and the sixth rule then tells you to prefer the cliché after all. The rules are not a method. They are a mood, and the last of them is the mood admitting it.

Take the rules' originality, of which there is none. Arnold Zwicky traced the passive prohibition to American composition handbooks of the early twentieth century, Strunk's Elements of Style of nineteen eighteen among the first, and found it a commonplace of the college classroom by the nineteen thirties. Orwell did not discover that plain prose was better than padded prose. He restated a schoolroom doctrine with more force and a more interesting politics, and the doctrine was already wrong in the ways it was wrong before he restated it.

And take the essay's reputation, which its own admirers have started to question. Steven Poole, a critic whose own book Unspeak is the modern descendant of Orwell's argument, has called this essay probably the most wildly overrated of any of his writings, and his objection is to the arbitrariness: a righteous but limited assault on political euphemism carried by a comically arbitrary collection of intolerances, as though a list of the words that irritated Orwell in nineteen forty-six were a theory of language. Ed Smith, in the New Statesman, made the sharper political point. Orwell thought obscurity was the technique of the liar. Smith suspects the opposite is now true: when a politician or a corporation needs to bridge the gap between what it is saying and what it knows, the preferred instrument is no longer the Latinate fog but a misleading simplicity, the short plain sentence that sounds like a man telling you the truth. The rules cannot see that at all. A liar who follows all six rules is a more convincing liar.

There it is, then. The rules are unoriginal, unfollowable, violated by their author at above the average rate, and blind to the form of political lying that has become standard since. If the essay were its rules, this episode would be a short one and the verdict would be Poole's.

Chapter Four: Steelman, Which Requires Reading the Whole Thing

The essay is not its rules, and the case for it starts with noticing where the rules are. They come in the second-to-last section, after the argument, offered as a practical aside for someone who has accepted the argument and wants to know what to do on Monday. Orwell says so himself, in the sentence before them, and he says something else that the style-guide readers never quote: look back through this essay, he writes, and you will find that he has again and again committed the very faults he is protesting against. Pullum's count does not embarrass a man who counted himself first. It confirms the essay's actual claim, which is that the habits are nearly impossible to escape, including for the person describing them, because they are not habits of style. They are habits of not thinking, and the essay is about thinking.

The argument, stripped of the rules, has three moves, and each is a mechanism rather than a preference. The first is that the causation runs both ways. Language becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, Orwell says, and then the half that matters: the slovenliness of the language makes it easier to have foolish thoughts. A dying metaphor is not merely dull. It is a phrase the writer did not have to think in order to produce, and a sentence assembled from phrases nobody thought is a sentence that nobody, including its author, has checked against anything. That is the clinical note from the first chapter. The patient was found to have deteriorated is a phrase that comes pre-assembled, and for that reason it arrives without the six hours in it, and the writer never has to decide to leave them out. The register decided.

The second move is the one about politics, and it is the sentence everyone quotes and almost nobody puts in context. Political language, Orwell writes, is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable. The context is a list, and the list is the mechanism. Defenceless villages are bombed from the air, their inhabitants driven into the countryside, their cattle machine-gunned, their huts set on fire: this is called pacification. Millions of peasants are robbed of their farms and sent trudging along the roads with what they can carry: this is called transfer of population. People are imprisoned without trial or shot in the back of the neck: this is called elimination of unreliable elements. Look at what the euphemism does in each case, and it is not what the rules imply. The Latinate phrase is not vaguer than the plain description in the sense of being less specific. It is just as specific. Everyone who used the phrase transfer of population in nineteen forty-six knew what it referred to. What the phrase removes is not the information but the image, and with the image goes the reflex, the flinch that a person would have if he had to say cattle machine-gunned aloud. The euphemism is a device for saying a true thing without having to feel it, and Orwell's argument is that a person who can say it that way can go on to do it that way, which is why political language and political atrocity keep the company they keep. The shelf met that mechanism last episode in the Soviet countryside. Transfer of population is what Scott's chapter on collectivisation looks like from inside the ministry that ordered it.

The third move is the one the essay is least credited for, and it is the one this series has been running on since its first episode. Orwell says that when you watch a tired hack on a platform mechanically repeating the familiar phrases, bestial atrocities, iron heel, bloodstained tyranny, you have the curious feeling that you are not watching a live human being but a dummy, and that the feeling becomes stronger at the moments when the light catches the speaker's spectacles and turns them into blank discs with no eyes behind them. A speaker who has gone over to phrases has stopped, for the duration of the speech, being a person who is choosing his words, and Orwell's word for what he has become is orthodoxy: a set of positions that can be uttered without the utterer having to be present. That is the organization man's interior surrender, seven episodes ago, seen from the outside, at the level of the sentence. Whyte's man gave his beliefs to the group and experienced it as belonging. Orwell's hack gives his sentences to the orthodoxy and experiences it as fluency. The Social Ethic was a prose style before it was a personality.

Chapter Five: The Mechanism Tested Against the Critics

Now put the critics against the argument rather than against the rules and see what happens.

Pullum's count is correct and it does not touch the mechanism. The passive is not the problem and Orwell, in the argument, never quite says it is; the rule is a crude proxy for something the argument states properly, which is that a sentence with no agent is a sentence in which nobody did anything. The patient was found to have deteriorated. Appropriate measures were instituted. Mistakes were made, the most famous three-word passive in American politics, is not bad because it is passive. It is bad since it has been constructed so that the question who made them has no place to attach. A passive with an agent is fine, and often necessary, and clinical prose has a hundred honest uses for it: the patient was randomised, the sample was centrifuged, where the agent is uninteresting and the process is what the sentence is for. The instrument is not the voice of the verb. It is whether the sentence has a slot for the person who would be responsible if the sentence were checked, and whether that slot has been filled. Orwell's rule four is a bad rule for a real thing, and Pullum has refuted the rule.

Poole's objection lands on the rules and slides off the argument for the same reason. The intolerances are arbitrary; the mechanism is not. A dying metaphor is a phrase the writer did not think; a pretentious word is a plain statement in a costume; a meaningless word is a claim that cannot be contradicted. Those are three ways of producing a sentence that cannot be checked, and Orwell's list of examples is a nineteen forty-six sample of each, and the sample is dated, and the categories are not. Anyone who has read a hospital's strategic plan can supply the twenty twenty-six sample without help.

Smith's objection is the one that actually costs something, and it should be conceded in full and then examined. Yes: plainness has been weaponised. The short sentence that sounds like a man telling the truth is the modern instrument of the man who is not. But look at what the plain-style liar's sentences have in common with the Latinate fog, and it is the thing the argument names. We got this wrong and we are fixing it. The plain sentence is agentless too; it just hides the agent in a we that has no address instead of in a passive that has none. It is checkable to the same degree as appropriate measures were instituted, which is not at all. Smith has shown that the rules cannot detect the modern lie. He has not shown that the mechanism cannot. The mechanism asks the same question of the short sentence that it asks of the long one: who, what, when, and what would I look at to find out whether this is so. The politician's plain style fails that question as completely as the professor's fog, and the essay, read for its argument rather than its list, told you it would.

Which leaves the count. The essay's rules are wrong, and its argument, that there is a kind of sentence which is built so that it cannot be checked, that such sentences are produced by not thinking and in turn make not thinking easier, and that they are the medium in which people say the unsayable to themselves first, is right and has not been answered. The linguists have won every engagement and lost the war, because they were fighting the wrong text.

Chapter Six: A Second Specimen, From a Grant

Orwell took his five specimens from the prose of nineteen forty-six, and the fair test of his categories is whether they still sort the prose of now, so here is a sixth, and I should say that it is constructed: not a real paragraph from a real application, but one assembled from the phrases that real applications are made of, in the way that Orwell assembled his Ecclesiastes translation. It reads like this. Leveraging a robust, multidisciplinary framework, the proposed initiative will facilitate the co-design of a scalable, community-driven intervention, optimising stakeholder engagement across the care continuum and generating actionable insights to inform sustainable, evidence-based transformation of service delivery.

Run the four categories over it. Dying metaphors: leveraging, which was a metaphor about a lever once and is now a way of not writing use; the care continuum, a line nobody has ever drawn. Verbal false limbs: facilitate the co-design of, where the plain verb is design and the padding exists to avoid saying who will do it; generating actionable insights to inform, which is four words standing in for find out. Pretentious diction: robust, multidisciplinary, scalable, sustainable, evidence-based, six adjectives that assert a quality without any of them naming a thing that could lack it. And meaningless words, which is where the sentence lives: stakeholder, engagement, transformation, initiative, words whose referent is agreed by nobody, so that the sentence can be neither confirmed nor contradicted by anything that subsequently happens in any clinic anywhere.

Now the essay's real test, the one from the first chapter. If a stranger wanted to find out whether that paragraph was true, what would they look at? There is nothing. No number, no place, no patient, no person who would be embarrassed if it failed, no description of what failure would even consist of. It cannot be wrong. And here is the part that makes the sixth specimen worse than Orwell's five: it was not produced by a hack on a platform. It was produced, in every real case the constructed one is built from, by an intelligent clinician who had a specific and checkable plan, a trial, a clinic, a population, a number of patients, an outcome that could be counted, and who translated it into that paragraph because that paragraph is the register the funding body's forms are written in, and because a committee reading forty applications will accept it without comment. The register did the concealing. The applicant signed. And a paragraph that cannot be wrong is, on the essay's argument, a paragraph in which nobody was thinking, which the applicant would deny, correctly, about the plan, and could not deny about the paragraph.

Chapter Seven: What the Shelf Owes This Essay

I should say plainly that this series is downstream of the essay in a way that no other book on the shelf can claim. The house charter for these scripts contains a list of banned phrases, and the list is an Orwellian document in the exact sense: a catalogue of the pre-assembled moves that let a narrator produce sentences he did not think. The aim is not plainness. Some of the best sentences on this shelf are long and Latinate. The aim is to catch the phrase that grades its own claim, the one that announces an insight as central or a sentence as structural before the listener has heard it, because a phrase like that is one the writer did not have to earn: an operator in Orwell's sense, a verbal false limb that tells the listener what to feel about a claim instead of showing him the claim and letting him feel it. Every episode of this feed is run through a list of those before it is published, and the list has grown as the listener has caught more of them, the essay's method applied to itself. Orwell said you would find the faults in his essay if you looked back through it. They are in this one too, and the difference is only that the looking is now done by a script, a fact about twenty twenty-six rather than about the argument.

And there is one place the essay's argument bites harder in a hospital than anywhere Orwell ever thought about, and it is the reason a clinician should read it. Medicine's register was built for the honest agentless sentence, the sample was centrifuged, and the register has been colonised by the dishonest one, appropriate measures were instituted, without the language changing at all. The same passive, the same Latin, the same institutional calm, and one of them is a method and the other is a defence. The only way to tell them apart is the question the essay hands you: can this be checked, and if not, who benefits from that. Every serious adverse event review I have ever read was an exercise in that question, and the sentences that had to be taken apart were never the ungrammatical ones. They were the fluent ones.

Chapter Eight: Verdict, Dose, and the Question for Monday

The verdict is that this is a flawed essay carrying an intact argument, and that it should be read for the argument and against the rules. Read the whole thing, not the excerpt; it is five thousand words and takes half an hour. Read Pullum on the passive and Poole on the intolerances the same day, and grant them everything, and then read the essay's middle section again, the list that runs from pacification to elimination of unreliable elements, and ask whether anything the critics said touched it. It did not. Do not pin the six rules to the wall. Pin the question.
