The dose is diagnostic, and it is cheaper than anything else on the shelf, because the instrument is a single question and it takes three seconds. This week, take one sentence from your own writing, a note, a report, a reply to a complaint, a paragraph in a grant, and ask of it: if a stranger wanted to find out whether this is true, what would they look at? If there is an answer, a date, a name, a number, a document, the sentence has an address and it can be wrong, and being able to be wrong is the only way a sentence can also be right. If nothing comes, if the sentence is true in the way that appropriate measures were instituted is true, then you have found the soft snow, and the useful discovery is not that you were lying. It is that you did not have to decide anything to produce it. The register decided, and you signed.

And the question for Monday is the one the essay asks of the tired hack and the shelf asks of every institution it has read: at what point in the sentence did the person stop being present? Find the phrase in your own organisation's official prose, the strategic plan, the incident report, the all-staff email, at which a person choosing words was replaced by an orthodoxy producing them, and then ask what that phrase was protecting the writer from having to see. It will be something. It was something in nineteen forty-six. Orwell's claim, which the linguists have not answered because they were never really addressing it, is that the something is where the politics is, and that the language was built to cover it, softly, like snow.

Next time, the shelf continues its Orwell series with the essay in which he shoots an animal he does not want to shoot because two thousand people are watching: Shooting an Elephant, on what a crowd does to the man with the gun. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Seeing Like a State (Scott) 2 of 2: collectivisation, ujamaa, metis, and the critics
item.description: Part two of two on James C. Scott's book – Soviet collectivisation and Tanzanian villagisation as the four conditions met in full, mētis as the name for what they destroyed, the four rules Scott offers instead, and the critics who think he stacked the deck.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Farm as a Factory

Part one ended on a question: what happens when the aesthetic that built Brasília is pointed not at where people live but at how they eat. Scott's first answer is the Soviet countryside between nineteen twenty-nine and nineteen thirty-three, and he opens it somewhere the listener will not expect, in the American West.

In the nineteen twenties the most admired farm in the world was in Montana. Thomas Campbell ran ninety-five thousand acres of wheat on land leased from the federal government, with tractors, combines, and a labour force organised in shifts, and he described what he was doing as industrial production that happened to take place outdoors. The Soviet leadership, which had never run a farm and distrusted everyone who had, found this irresistible. Lenin had already written admiringly of Taylorism, the American doctrine that any job could be broken into timed motions and reassembled by an engineer, and had proposed that the Soviet state adopt it wholesale; the German war economy of nineteen seventeen, in which the state had directed industry as a single machine, was his other model. The idea that agriculture could be the same, a factory with fields for a floor, ran straight through the Bolshevik imagination, and Campbell was invited to the Soviet Union in nineteen twenty-nine to advise on the largest farm ever attempted, a state grain enterprise near Rostov, hundreds of thousands of acres, that was named, without irony, Gigant.

Scott's point in beginning there is that collectivisation was not, at its root, a Marxist idea. It was a high-modernist one, and it was shared. The American agronomists who visited the Soviet Union in those years were often as enchanted by the scale of the state farms as the Soviets were by the Montana wheat; the difference was that the Americans had no power to impose the vision on unwilling farmers, and the Soviets did. The four conditions from part one were all present at once for the first time in the book: the administrative ordering of nature and society, the ideology that made it a mission, a state willing to use unlimited coercion, and a peasantry that had already been broken once, in the civil war, and had no organised means of refusing.

What was imposed had two logics, and Scott is careful to keep them apart. The first was the factory logic: enormous farms, uniform crops, mechanisation, a work force treated as labour rather than as farmers, a plan issued from Moscow specifying what was to be sown where. The second was older and simpler and, in his reading, the one that actually drove the policy: legibility for appropriation. The Soviet state needed grain, to feed the cities and to sell abroad for the machinery its industrialisation required, and it could not extract it from twenty-five million scattered peasant households whose harvests it could not see and whose surpluses they hid. It could get grain from a few hundred thousand collective farms with a manager, a ledger, and a procurement quota. The kolkhoz, the collective farm, was, before it was anything else, a device for making the harvest visible and collectable. Scott's word for what the peasants received in exchange is precise: it was a second serfdom, with the state as the landlord, an internal passport system to keep the farmers on the land, and a quota that came first, before the farm's own food.

The outcome is known and the shelf should say it plainly, because Scott does. Between nineteen thirty-two and nineteen thirty-three, in Ukraine, the Volga, Kazakhstan, and the North Caucasus, somewhere between five and nine million people starved to death, while grain continued to be procured and, in some years, exported. Livestock numbers fell by half or more as peasants slaughtered animals rather than surrender them. The gigantic farms, Gigant included, proved unmanageable and were broken up within a few years. What survived, for sixty years, was the collective farm as a procurement machine, and what kept it fed, Scott notes, was the thing the plan had left out: the private plots, the small gardens each household was eventually permitted to keep, which occupied a few percent of the land and produced, by the later decades, a large fraction of the country's vegetables, fruit, eggs, and meat. The illegible remainder fed the legible system.

Chapter Two: The Village Drawn on a Map

The Tanzanian case is the one Scott thinks is most instructive, because the people who ran it were not monsters. Julius Nyerere was a schoolteacher, a Catholic, a democrat by the standards of post-colonial Africa, and by any account a man who wanted his country's peasants to be better off. Ujamaa, the policy he announced in the Arusha Declaration of nineteen sixty-seven, means something like familyhood in Swahili, and its founding idea was that Tanzania's scattered rural population should live together in villages where the state could bring them schools, clinics, clean water, and agricultural advice, and where they could farm cooperatively. Nobody who reads the declaration doubts the sincerity of it.

For six years the villages were voluntary, and not many people moved. So in nineteen seventy-three the government made it compulsory, and between then and nineteen seventy-six, in what Scott describes as by most accounts the largest forced resettlement in independent Africa to that date, at least five million Tanzanians were moved, often by lorry, sometimes with their old houses burned behind them so that they could not return, into villages laid out by officials. The layouts are the detail that connects this chapter to Brasília. The new villages were drawn on a grid, houses in rows along a road, identical plots, the fields in blocks beyond, so that from the road, and from the district office, and from the capital, a village looked like a village should look: orderly, countable, visitable. Scott's title for the chapter is Compulsory Villagisation in Tanzania: Aesthetics and Miniaturisation, and the second word carries the chapter. Unable to make the whole countryside legible at once, the state built miniatures of legibility, model villages that could be shown to visiting ministers, and then required the country to live in them.

What the grid could not see was how Tanzanian farmers had been feeding themselves. Across much of the country the practice was polycropping: several crops planted together in the same field, at different heights, maturing at different times, some for food, some for cash, some to fix nitrogen, some as insurance against the failure of the others. To an agronomist trained on temperate monocultures this looked like a mess, and the state's agricultural officers, most of whom had that training, said so. The villages were laid out for single crops in straight rows, which the extension services could inspect, and the farmers were moved away from the land they knew, its soils and its water and its risks, to land the planners had selected for its position on the road. The result was what a listener who has heard part one will predict: yields fell, food had to be imported, the villages' cooperative fields were neglected while the farmers walked back, sometimes for hours, to their old plots, and by the end of the decade the state had stopped enforcing most of what it had built. Nobody starved in millions. What was lost was slower and, for the book's argument, more exact: a body of practice that had taken generations to build, dismantled in three years by people who did not know it was there, because the only thing they had been trained to see was the row.

And Scott adds the observation about Tanzania that stops it being a story about Africa. Almost every element of ujamaa had been tried before, by the British colonial administration in the nineteen forties and fifties, with the same aesthetic and the same failures, and the independent government had inherited the files. The colonial officers had wanted legible villages for tax and control; the socialist government wanted them for services and cooperation; the grid was the same grid. The politics changed and the way of seeing did not, and that is the book's argument in one country: high modernism is not a political programme but a set of eyes, and it can be worn by a colonial governor and the man who replaced him.

Chapter Three: The Word for What Was Lost

Now the chapter the whole book has been walking toward, and the word the shelf will keep. Scott needs a name for the thing the forestry tables, the Soviet plan, and the Tanzanian grid all failed to see, and he finds it in Greek. Mētis is the quality Odysseus has: cunning, practical, adaptive intelligence, the knowledge of how to respond to a situation that is never the same twice. The Greeks set it against technē, the kind of knowledge that can be written as rules and taught in a classroom, and Scott's claim is that most of what keeps any complex human activity working is the first kind and that the state, by its nature, can only see the second.

The examples are the best in the book, and two of them belong in the ear. The first is the harbour pilot. A ship's captain knows how to sail the open sea, and that knowledge is largely technē: charts, instruments, rules of navigation, the same everywhere. When the ship reaches a harbour, the captain hands the wheel to a pilot who knows this harbour, its shoals and currents and the way the wind comes off that particular headland at that particular hour, and the pilot's knowledge is not in any book, because it cannot be. It is the accumulated experience of a lifetime spent in one place, revised daily, and it is worth more, in that harbour, than the captain's whole education. The second example is a farmer's rule, and Scott uses it because it looks like nonsense. An old piece of New England planting advice, attributed to the Native American practice the settlers learned from, says to plant corn when the oak leaves are the size of a squirrel's ear. An agronomist would replace that with a soil temperature and a calendar date. But the calendar date is wrong in a late spring and the soil thermometer requires a thermometer, and the oak leaf integrates, without instruments, everything about the season that matters to a seed, in the one place where the seed is going to be planted. The rule is not primitive. It is a compression of local experience into a form a person can carry, and it is more accurate than the formula that would replace it, in the cases where accuracy matters most.

That is the argument, and it needs to be stated carefully because it is easy to state badly. Scott is not saying that local knowledge is always right or that science is always wrong; he says so several times, and his critics would say he does not say it loudly enough. He is saying that mētis is a different kind of knowledge, that it lives in practice rather than in documents, that it is destroyed when the practice is disrupted, and that a state which can only read documents will not detect the destruction until the second rotation. The forest's ants, the peasant's private plot, the Tanzanian field with five crops in it, the harbour pilot: none of them can be put in a report, so nobody can defend them in the meeting where the report is discussed.

Here the shelf's own instruments engage, and the join is with the last two books. Graeber's interpretive labour was the work the powerless do to make themselves legible to the powerful. Mētis is what that work costs when it succeeds: the villager who learns to describe his fields in the planner's categories has stopped describing the fields, and the planner now has a document that says the wrong thing in the right format. And Bullshit Jobs, two episodes ago, found a workforce paid to produce documents nobody reads. Scott's book suggests why that workforce exists. An institution that can only see documents will pay to have the world converted into documents, whether or not the conversion loses the thing that mattered, because to the institution the document is the thing. The box ticker is a legibility machine. What he ticks is the row the state can see.

Chapter Four: What Scott Actually Recommends

The book's last chapter is short and it is the one the book's admirers on the right tend to skip, because it does not say what they want it to. Scott does not recommend abolishing planning, or the state, or expertise. He recommends four rules for anyone who has to intervene in a complex system they do not fully understand, and they are worth stating exactly, because they are the closest the shelf has yet come to an antidote that survives its own diagnosis.

Take small steps. In a system you cannot see whole, the intervention should be small enough that its effects can be observed before the next one is made. Favour reversibility. Prefer the change that can be undone if it proves wrong; a grid can be drawn on a map in an afternoon and cannot be un-drawn from a countryside in a generation. Plan on surprises. Assume the system will respond in ways the plan did not anticipate, and build the plan so that the surprises can be accommodated rather than suppressed. And plan on human inventiveness: assume the people inside will adapt whatever is imposed on them, and design the imposition so that their adaptations improve it rather than sabotage it, which means leaving them room to adapt at all.

A clinician will recognise those rules, because they are the rules of prescribing. Start low, go slow; prefer the drug you can stop; expect the side effect you did not predict; and assume the patient will do something unintended with the prescription, so write it in a form that survives that. Scott's rules are the same instinct scaled up to a state, and the reason they are radical is that they run against the grain of everything a planning institution is built to do. A ministry is rewarded for a plan that is large, complete, and irreversible, because that is what a plan looks like when it is presented to a minister, and a plan with room in it for the villagers to change it is, from the ministry's chair, an unfinished plan.

And the four rules are also, and this is the observation that ties the series together, the reverse of the four conditions. Against the full administrative ordering of society, small steps. Against an ideology that makes the plan a mission, plan on being wrong. Against an authority willing to use unlimited force, prefer what can be undone. And against a prostrate civil society, count on the people to invent, which is only possible if they have been left standing. Scott's antidote is not a different plan. It is the withdrawal, one at a time, of the conditions under which any plan becomes a catastrophe.

Chapter Five: The Case Against, With the Historians Attached

The critics should be heard at full strength, and this book has better critics than most, because it made large claims in fields where people had spent their lives.

The first count comes from the Soviet historians, and it is the one that should worry an admirer most. Mark Tauger, who has spent a career on the harvests of the nineteen thirties, reviewed the book for H-Net in nineteen ninety-nine under a title that gives his objection away, The Moral Agronomy of the Peasant versus the Moral Economy of the Town. Tauger's charge is that Scott's account of collectivisation leaves out the harvests. The famine of nineteen thirty-two and thirty-three, in his reconstruction, was set off by a genuine crop failure, drought and disease and weather, on top of which the state's procurement policy and its export commitments in the middle of a world depression turned shortage into mass death. Legibility and high modernism are part of the story; they are not, he argues, the mechanism, and a book that makes them the mechanism is telling a morality tale in which the state is always the actor and the weather never is. He adds that the collective farms, for all their horrors, had by the end of the decade restored grain output to something like pre-revolutionary levels through mechanisation and inputs, which is not a fact Scott's argument has a place for. The same omission, Tauger says, recurs in Tanzania: the food shortages of the nineteen seventies had causes, drought and the oil shock among them, that were not villagisation, and Scott does not weigh them.

That is a real objection, and it is the historian's version of the one this shelf keeps raising: what is the denominator, and what would have happened anyway. Scott's method is the case study, and a case study can show that a mechanism operated. It cannot, on its own, show how much of the outcome the mechanism explains, and the book does not try. The listener should hold the collectivisation chapter as a demonstration that the state's way of seeing made the famine possible and made it worse, and should not hold it as the finding that it caused the famine, because that claim needs a counterfactual Scott does not supply.

The second count is about the deck. Scott Alexander, in a long and admiring review that has done more than any academic review to carry the book to a new generation, ends by objecting that the book stacks the dice against high modernism. Every case is a failure. The Green Revolution, which applied the very kind of top-down agronomic science Scott distrusts and roughly doubled cereal yields across Asia, is not in the book. Nor are sewers, vaccination, the abolition of the medieval city's actual filth; the standard measures that disarmed the landlord are conceded and then set aside. And Alexander puts his finger on the problem the mētis chapter never resolves: how do you tell evolved local wisdom from people resisting a beneficial change for ordinary reasons of habit and interest? The oak leaf is charming. So, presumably, were a great many local practices about disease that killed people for centuries until a legible, uniform, state-imposed intervention stopped them. Scott's framework can name the second kind of case; the book does not contain one.

The third count is the one the first episode of this pair promised, and it comes from an economist. Brad DeLong, reviewing the book, made the observation that its argument about local knowledge and the limits of central planning is Friedrich Hayek's argument, made in the nineteen forties, and that Scott, who mentions Hayek barely at all, seems unable to make contact with his own intellectual roots. If mētis is dispersed knowledge that no central authority can collect, DeLong says, then the institution that already exists to aggregate dispersed knowledge without anyone collecting it is the price system, and a book that arrives at Hayek's diagnosis and then declines Hayek's prescription owes the reader a reason. Scott's reason, given at the end of the book and at length in a Cato Unbound exchange in twenty ten, is that large market actors see like states too: the supermarket chain that requires a tomato bred to survive shipping rather than to taste of anything has done to the tomato what the forester did to the forest, and it did it with no ministry involved. The political theorist Henry Farrell took DeLong up on that point, arguing that market standardisation and state standardisation advance together and that DeLong's revealed-preference reply, that people bought the rubber tomato because it was cheap, misses how the institutions that sell it shape what people are able to prefer. The dispute is not settled, and this shelf's own finding leans toward Scott: the Davies series found the corporation running on procedures no one controls, seeing its customers as rows in a system, in ways the Unaccountability Machine episodes catalogued with no state anywhere in the story. But DeLong's count stands as a demand the book never met. If you believe in mētis, you owe an account of which institutions preserve it, and Scott's book is far better at naming the ones that destroy it.

And a fourth, briefer count, from the political scientist David Laitin among others: the evidence is selective. Scott chose the cases that show the mechanism, and told them beautifully, and a reader who wants to know how often the mechanism operates, out of how many state projects, has been given a museum rather than a survey. This is the same objection as Tauger's in a different accent, and the shelf has met it twice this season, in Graeber's testimonies and in Freeman's single group. The case series proves the condition exists. It does not tell you the rate.

Chapter Six: The Lean

Set the critics beside the shelf's most recent instrument and something uncomfortable appears. Three episodes ago Orwell audited Burnham by lining up his forecasts and reading the direction of the misses, and found that a mind enchanted by power reads the winners as the future. Run the same audit on Scott. Every case in the book resolves the same way: the state plans, the plan fails, the local knowledge was right. The misses, if they are misses, all lean toward the village. And Scott's later career confirms the direction: his next books were on the peoples of upland Southeast Asia who had spent two thousand years evading states altogether, and then a history of the earliest states as a catastrophe for the people who fell under them, and the title of one of them was, in so many words, The Art of Not Being Governed. This is a man whose instrument detects one kind of error superbly and is not built to detect its opposite.

That is not a refutation. Orwell's audit, the fourth episode of this run established, cannot distinguish a lean from a long-horizon call, and the thing that separates them is whether the forecaster has a mechanism. Scott has one, and it is a good one: institutions that can only read documents will destroy what does not fit in documents, and will not know they have done it until the second rotation. What the lean tells you is where to be careful. When Scott says the state's vision failed, believe him; he has shown you the mechanism a dozen times. When he implies the local practice would have been fine if left alone, check, because that is the claim his instrument cannot test and his temperament will not.

Chapter Seven: Verdict, Dose, and the Question for Monday

The verdict is that this is the book on the shelf that goes deepest into the question the series actually cares about, and that it should be read with its critics in the same week. Every earlier book found an organization failing at something it could see: multiplying its staff, promoting its wrong people, absorbing its complaints. Scott's finding is prior to all of those. The organization fails first at seeing, and the failure is not a defect but the price of being an organization at all, because a body that governs at scale can only govern what it has simplified, and the simplification discards, by construction, the knowledge that lived in the detail. That finding survives Tauger and Alexander and DeLong. What does not survive them is the book's silence about the other direction: the cases where the simplification saved lives, and the question of which institutions, if not the state, keep mētis alive. Hold the mechanism. Distrust the museum.

The dose is diagnostic and specific. Read the forestry chapter and the mētis chapter whole; read the Brasília chapter for pleasure; read the collectivisation chapter with Tauger's review open beside it, and read Alexander's review after, for the objection the book most needs and least wants. Then read Scott's four rules and pin them somewhere. They are the only antidote on this shelf so far that does not require anyone to be better than they are.

And the question for Monday comes straight from the four rules, pointed at whatever your institution is currently planning. Take the plan, the reorganisation, the new pathway, the dashboard, the merger of two services into one, and ask the four questions in order. Is it small enough that you will see what it does before the next step is taken? Can it be undone in less time than it took to build? Has anyone written down what would count as the plan being wrong? And what have the people who will live inside it been left free to change? If the answers are no, no, no, and nothing, then you are looking at a scientific forest in its first rotation, and the yields will be magnificent, and you should find out now who is going to be reintroducing the ants.

Next time, the shelf returns to Orwell, and to the essay everyone quotes and almost nobody has read carefully: Politics and the English Language, with the linguists who think it is nonsense and the case for why the mechanism is true anyway. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Seeing Like a State (Scott) 1 of 2: legibility, high modernism, planned cities
item.description: Part one of two on James C. Scott's 1998 book – how a state makes the world readable to itself, why the reading is always a simplification, and what happened when the simplifications were built in timber, in tax rolls, and in concrete on a Brazilian plateau.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Second Rotation

In the last decades of the eighteenth century the states of Prussia and Saxony had a problem that every treasury recognises. Wood was the fuel, the building material, and the ship of the age, and the crown's forests were producing it in amounts nobody could state. A forest, to the people who lived beside it, was a place of grazing, foraging, firewood, medicine, game, thatch, bark, and resin, used by dozens of overlapping customary rights that no clerk had ever written down. To the fiscal officer in the capital it was a source of revenue with an unknown yield, and therefore a source of anxiety. And so the officer's profession invented a discipline, scientific forestry, whose first act was to redescribe the forest as one thing. Not a habitat, not a commons: a quantity of saleable timber, standing, per hectare, per year.

The redescription started as an accounting method and became a landscape. Foresters sampled plots, counted trees, sorted them into size classes, and built tables from which the yield of a whole forest could be computed from its area, and the tables were so much easier to use on a uniform forest that the profession began to grow uniform forests. Old mixed woodland was cleared. In its place, in rows, at fixed spacing, all of one age, went a single species selected for how fast it turned sunlight into board feet, most often Norway spruce. The underbrush was cleared because underbrush is not timber. The dead wood was removed because dead wood is not timber. What resulted was a forest a clerk could read from a desk: so many trees, so many years, so much revenue, and the first rotation, the first crop of trees to grow from seedling to harvest, was magnificent. Yields came in as predicted. The method was adopted across Europe, then exported to the colonies and to the United States, and the foresters who had designed it were, in the ordinary way of these things, promoted.

The second rotation failed. Trees planted in the same rows on the same ground grew slower, sickened more, and blew down more readily, and the decline was steep enough that German forestry acquired a word for it, Waldsterben, forest death. It took the better part of a century to understand why, and the reason is the book in one paragraph. The old forest had been doing an enormous amount of work that did not appear in the tables. The dead wood and the underbrush had been feeding the soil; the mixed species had been sharing the pests and the wind between them; the birds and the insects and the fungi that a spruce plantation could not support had been the forest's maintenance crew. The tables had not measured any of that because none of it was timber, and the forest had been rebuilt to match the tables. What the foresters had been managing, for one rotation, was a bank balance drawn on capital they could not see. When the capital ran out they were reduced to what Scott calls, with some relish, restoration forestry: reintroducing, by hand, in boxes, the ant colonies and spiders and birds' nests whose removal nobody had recorded, because their presence had never been written down.

Hold that story, because the book you are about to hear about is a long argument that the forest is what a state does to everything it looks at. The series has spent sixteen episodes inside organizations asking where their competence goes. This book turns the question around and asks what an organization can see in the first place, and it answers that the seeing is the problem, before any of the failures the shelf has catalogued have a chance to occur.

Chapter Two: An Anarchist at Yale

James C. Scott, for the listener who needs the biography, spent his career at Yale as a professor of political science and anthropology, and spent his intellectual life on the losing side of the encounter between states and the people they govern. His early books, The Moral Economy of the Peasant in nineteen seventy-six and Weapons of the Weak in nineteen eighty-five, were fieldwork among Southeast Asian villagers, and the second of them is where the book you are hearing about was born. He had gone to Malaysia to study how peasants resisted, expecting revolts, and found instead foot-dragging, false compliance, pilfering, slander, sabotage, and a stubborn refusal to be counted, which he came to see as the ordinary politics of people who cannot afford open politics. Seeing Like a State, published by Yale in nineteen ninety-eight, is the view from the other side of that encounter: what the state was trying to do, why it kept failing, and why it never stopped trying. Its subtitle is How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed, and the word certain is doing careful work, which the second part of this pair will come back to.

One more thing about the author, because it shapes the reading. Scott called himself, half-seriously, an anarchist, and wrote a later book called Two Cheers for Anarchism, and the two cheers rather than three are characteristic. He was not against states. He was against a particular kind of confidence states acquire, and he was equally suspicious of large corporations, which he thought saw like states too. The distinction has consequences, because the book has been claimed since by people to Scott's right, who read it as an argument for markets against planning, and Scott spent a good deal of his later life explaining that he had not written that book. Whether he had, in fact, is one of the questions for part two.

Chapter Three: Legibility

The book's first word for what the foresters did is legibility, and it is the word the shelf will keep. A state, in Scott's account, has one problem before all others: it cannot see its own territory. It wants to tax, conscript, and prevent rebellion, and every one of those requires knowing who is where, owning what, producing how much, and the society it faces has been built by people with no interest in being known. Local practice is dense, particular, and illegible from the capital. Land is held in overlapping customary tenures that make sense to the village and to nobody else; people are known by names that change with the season, the trade, and the father; grain is measured in baskets whose size depends on the district and, in bad years, on the goodwill of the person filling them. To govern that, the state has to simplify it, and the simplification is not a description of what is there. It is a replacement.

The examples are the pleasure of the book, and three of them belong in the ear. The first is the surname. For most of history most people did not have one; they had a given name and a set of local descriptors, John the smith, John by the mill, John son of Tom, which worked perfectly for people who knew John and were useless to a tax collector who did not. Permanent, inherited surnames were, in almost every case Scott traces, a state project: the Florentine catasto of the fourteen twenties, which needed to attach households to their tax assessments across years; the Spanish administration of the Philippines, which in eighteen forty-nine issued a catalogue of surnames and assigned them to the population alphabetically by district, so that a modern map of Filipino surnames still reproduces the order of the pages; the Prussian and Napoleonic states requiring their Jewish subjects to adopt fixed family names as a condition of civil status. A surname is a handle the state can hold you by. Once you have one, you can be found next year.

The second example is measurement. A pre-modern bushel was not a quantity; it was a relationship. The basket was heaped or levelled, struck or shaken down, according to who was paying whom and what the custom of the district had negotiated over generations, and every one of those variations encoded something a local person understood and an outsider could not. The metric system, born in the French Revolution, was among other things an act of state vision: one metre, one litre, one kilogram, everywhere, forever, so that a report from any district could be read against one from anywhere else. Scott is careful to say that this was often a liberation. A landlord who could shrink the peasant's bushel at will was a landlord the metre disarmed. But the same reform that disarmed him made the peasant's grain readable to Paris, which had its own uses for it.

The third is the cadastral map, the survey that draws property as bounded parcels with a single owner and a number, so that the parcel can be taxed and, when the time comes, sold. Scott's argument is that the map does not record land tenure. It creates a land tenure that the map can record. Every overlapping right, the widow's gleaning, the village's grazing after harvest, the neighbour's path, is either written onto the map as a formal encumbrance, which rarely happens, or vanishes from the legal world, which usually does. The forest again: the map is the yield table, and the countryside is rebuilt to match it.

Here is where this book joins the shelf's running argument, and the join is close. Two episodes ago The Utopia of Rules described interpretive labour: in any relationship of unequal power, the party with less power carries the burden of understanding the other, translating themselves into the other's categories, because the party with more power does not have to bother. Scott has found the state-sized version. Legibility is interpretive labour imposed from above at the scale of a whole society, the population obliged to present itself in forms the capital can read, and the capital under no obligation to learn the population's forms in return. Graeber called the result structural stupidity, and Scott's forests are what structural stupidity looks like when it has a budget and a surveying team. But Scott adds the half Graeber did not have. The simplifications are not merely a convenience for power. They are, most of the time, the only way a large state can function at all. A state that could not count would not be a gentler state; it would be one unable to vaccinate, could not run a court, could not deliver a pension. The problem is not that the map is simpler than the territory. Every map is. The problem arrives when the people holding the map forget that, and begin to treat the territory's departures from the map as errors in the territory.

Chapter Four: The Grid

Scott has a pair of maps early in the book that I would put in front of anyone who wants the argument in one glance. The first is Bruges around fifteen hundred: a tangle of streets that curve, fork, narrow, and dead-end, a city that has grown the way a coral grows, by accretion, each street the trace of some decision made by people who lived on it. The second is Chicago in the eighteen nineties: a grid, every block the same, every street numbered, so regular that a stranger can find any address in the city from the address alone. Scott's point is not that one is good and one bad. It is that they are legible to different people. Bruges is legible to its residents and opaque to everyone else; a stranger without a guide is lost within three turns, and so, usefully, is an invading army or a tax assessor. Chicago is legible to the stranger, the assessor, the surveyor, the fire brigade, and the real-estate lawyer, and it is legible from the map, which means it can be governed from the map by people who have never walked it.

The grid was, in the American case, a deliberate instrument of exactly that kind. Manhattan's commissioners' plan of eighteen eleven laid twelve avenues and one hundred and fifty-five cross streets over an island that was still mostly farms, hills, and streams, and the commissioners were candid that the reason was that right-angled houses are the cheapest to build and the easiest to sell. The plan ignored the topography entirely; the hills were to be levelled and the streams filled, and they were. What resulted was a city that could be subdivided, taxed, and traded in identical parcels by anyone with a copy of the plan, which was the intention, and a city whose one great irregular space, Central Park, had to be carved out later, against the grid, once it became obvious what the grid could not provide. The grid is the forestry table drawn on land: a redescription of a place as a set of interchangeable units, which then becomes the place.

And there is a darker case that Scott raises and does not dwell on, and the shelf should, because it is the example that stops the argument being merely about efficiency. A legible population is a population that can be found. The Netherlands entered the Second World War with one of the best civil registration systems in Europe, complete, accurate, and cross-referenced by address and religion, built over decades for the ordinary and benign purposes of a modern state. When the occupying authorities wanted to locate the country's Jews, the registers gave them the list. In France, whose records were worse, and in Belgium, where the registry offices were in some cases sabotaged by their own staff, the proportion of the Jewish population who were found and deported was much lower. Nobody who built the Dutch registers intended that use. The registers did not care what was intended. Legibility is a capacity, and a capacity, once built, belongs to whoever holds the state, a truth about states rather than about the Dutch, and it is the reason Scott's suspicion of the map is not a sentimental preference for medieval streets. The tangle that frustrates the assessor frustrates the police just as well.

That is the cost side of the ledger, and it should be stated as plainly as the benefit side was a moment ago. The metre disarmed the landlord and the surname enabled the pension, and the same instruments located the deportees and levelled the hills. There is no version of the instrument that does only the first. The question the book is really asking, from here on, is what determines which use a state makes of the vision it has built, and Scott's answer is the four conditions that the next chapter names.

Chapter Five: High Modernism

Scott gives that forgetting a name, and the name is the second word the shelf will keep: high modernism. He means by it something more specific than modernity and more dangerous than planning. It is a faith, at its height between roughly eighteen ninety and the nineteen sixties, that the same scientific rationality which had produced the railway and the vaccine could be applied to the design of whole societies, and that the designer, armed with that rationality, was entitled to override the objections of the people being designed, because the objections were, by definition, pre-scientific. High modernism is not left or right. Scott's examples include Lenin and Le Corbusier, Robert McNamara and Walther Rathenau, the Soviet agronomist and the American highway engineer, and what they share is an aesthetic rather than a politics: a love of straight lines, grids, uniformity, and the view from above, and a corresponding contempt for the tangle that any living settlement presents when you walk through it at ground level.

Now the book's method becomes visible, and it should be named because it is the thing Scott is best at. He does not argue that high modernists were wicked. Most of them were sincere, some were brilliant, and their goals, housing for the poor, food for the hungry, a city without slums, were goals any decent person shared. His argument is that the aesthetic did the damage regardless of the intention, because the aesthetic determined what the planner could see, and that turned out to be the plan. The tangle at ground level, which is where all the information about how a place actually works is stored, registered to the high-modernist eye as disorder, and disorder was what the plan existed to abolish.

Scott then supplies the framework that the rest of the book is a series of applications of, and it is worth stating exactly because the second part of this pair will need it. Legibility alone is not a catastrophe. Every modern state simplifies, and most survive it. High modernism alone is not a catastrophe either; an architect with a grid and no power builds an unpleasant building. The disasters the book is about require four things together: the administrative ordering of nature and society, the high-modernist ideology that makes the ordering a moral mission, an authoritarian state willing and able to use its full coercive power to realise the design, and a prostrate civil society that lacks the capacity to resist. Take away any one and the failure is smaller, or recoverable, or never happens. Put all four together and the plan gets built exactly as drawn, and the forest's second rotation arrives for people.

Chapter Six: The Straight Street

Before the book gets to the cases where all four conditions were met, it stops in cities, and the city chapter is the one I would have a listener keep if they kept one, because it is where the argument can be checked against a place you can visit.

Begin with Paris under Haussmann, between eighteen fifty-three and eighteen seventy. Napoleon the Third's prefect cut boulevards through the medieval city, straight, wide, and long, and the official reasons were circulation, sanitation, and light, all of which were real; the Paris he inherited was crowded, sick, and dark. But the boulevards had a second logic that Scott reads out of their geometry. A straight wide street is a street a regiment can march down and a cannon can fire along, and the quarters the boulevards cut through were, not by coincidence, the quarters that had thrown up barricades in eighteen thirty and eighteen forty-eight. Legibility again: the state could now see, and reach, parts of its own capital that had been dark to it. The modern Paris everyone loves is, among other things, the map imposed on the city so that the city could be governed from the map.

Then Le Corbusier, who is high modernism with a drafting pencil. His Plan Voisin of nineteen twenty-five proposed demolishing the centre of Paris north of the Seine and replacing it with eighteen identical cruciform towers in a park, connected by motorways, with the functions of the city, living, working, shopping, moving, sorted into separate zones so that each could be designed to its single purpose. The plan was never built, and that is the only reason we can still visit Paris. But its principles were, in whole or part, in a great many places, and Scott's reading of the principles is exact: they are the yield table applied to human settlement. A city is redescribed as a set of quantities, dwellings per hectare, cubic metres of air per person, minutes of travel to work, and then rebuilt so that the quantities are optimal. The redescription leaves out the same things the forestry tables left out. It leaves out everything that happens in a street because streets have corners, and shops have doorsteps, and children play where adults can see them, and a neighbour notices a stranger, and a thousand small unplanned encounters keep a neighbourhood safe, useful, and alive. Le Corbusier's contempt for the street was explicit: he thought the corridor street a relic, and he thought the people who liked it were sentimental.

The book's counter-witness is Jane Jacobs, whose Death and Life of Great American Cities in nineteen sixty-one is Scott's anthology of what the plan cannot see, and here the series' two most recent books meet. Jacobs walked the streets Le Corbusier would have demolished and catalogued what they were doing: mixed use, so that the street was populated at every hour by different people for different reasons; short blocks, so that paths crossed; old buildings beside new, so that rents varied and the cheap ones housed the things a neighbourhood needed but could not pay much for; density, so that eyes were on the street. None of that was in any plan, because it had not been planned. It had accreted, the way the old forest accreted, by the trial and error of people who used the place daily and adjusted it a doorstep at a time. Jacobs never gave the missing thing a single name. Scott does, and he saves it for the second half: the practical, local, unwritten knowledge of how a particular place works, mētis, after the Greek word for the cunning of Odysseus, and which the second part of this pair will spend a chapter on.

Chapter Seven: The City Built in Four Years

Brasília is where Scott lets the aesthetic build its perfect object, because in Brasília it was allowed to. In nineteen fifty-six the Brazilian president Juscelino Kubitschek decided to move the capital from Rio to an empty plateau in the interior, and to do it within his term. The plan was Lúcio Costa's, a great cross of two axes laid on the empty ground, one monumental, for government, one residential, curved like a wing; the buildings were Oscar Niemeyer's, and both men were disciples of Le Corbusier. The city was designed whole, on paper, before anyone lived there, with the functions sorted into sectors, a hotel sector, a banking sector, a residential sector of identical superblocks, each superblock a set of identical apartment buildings on stilts in open ground, so that from the air the whole city read as a single legible diagram, which it does to this day. It was inaugurated in nineteen sixty, four years after the decision. It is, by common consent, one of the most beautiful things ever photographed from an aircraft.

What Scott describes is what it is like on the ground, and he leans on the anthropologist James Holston, who lived there and wrote The Modernist City. The plan had abolished the street. There were no corners, because the superblocks were set in open space; no doorsteps, because the buildings stood on pillars; no crowds, because the sectors had sorted the crowd's reasons for existing into separate districts miles apart; no small shops beneath the apartments, because commerce had its own sector. The residents developed a word, brasilite, Brasília-itis, for the condition of living there, and Holston's informants described it as the absence of the small pleasures of city life, the crowd, the chance meeting, the sense that a place was being used. People who could afford to left for the satellite towns that grew up, unplanned and illegible, around the plan's edge, which is where most of the capital's population has lived ever since. The planned city was built, exactly as drawn. The city that people wanted to live in built itself, next to it, the way the underbrush comes back in the plantation.

And here is the observation that makes Brasília the book's hinge rather than one more example. The plan did not fail because it was badly executed. It was executed superbly, on time, by gifted people, and the failure is the execution. Every previous book on this shelf has found competence leaking out of an organization somewhere between intention and result: Parkinson's paperwork, Peter's final placements, the sinks that absorb what nobody wanted to know. Scott's cases invert that. Brasília is what happens when nothing leaks, when a plan meets an authority strong enough to carry it out without friction and a population unable to resist. The competence was all there. It was pointed at a picture of a city rather than at a city, and no amount of competence corrects that, because the correction would have had to come from the ground, and the ground was the thing the picture could not see.

Chapter Eight: What the Shelf Now Has, and What It Still Needs

Set this half of the book beside the last two episodes and a shape appears that neither Graeber nor Orwell had on their own. Orwell caught Burnham predicting a continuation of whatever was happening, and diagnosed the lean: a mind enchanted by power reads the present as the future. Scott's high modernist has a lean of the same family running the other way. He does not read the present as the future; he reads the plan as the present, and everything in the present that fails to match the plan as noise. Burnham's error was to trust the map of the winners. The planner's error is to trust a map he drew himself, which is a harder error to catch, because the map is very good, and because the person best placed to catch it, the villager or the resident or the forester's labourer, has been defined in advance as the person whose knowledge does not count.

And Graeber's structural stupidity, which two episodes ago looked like a moral failing of the powerful, now looks like something closer to a design constraint. A state cannot govern what it cannot read, and the tangle cannot be read without being simplified, and the simplification will always leave out the things that are hardest to write down, which are, as a rule, the things that keep the place alive. That is not a claim about bad people. It is about what a large organization is, and it lands, for this series, as a limit on every antidote the shelf has yet to consider. Whatever repair the later books propose, rotation, rival power, formal addresses for complaints, the repair will be administered by an institution that sees like a state, and its first act will be to make the problem legible enough to repair, which is where the trouble began.

The question part one leaves on the table is the one the four conditions pose, and it is a question about people rather than trees or streets. Brasília cost money and comfort; nobody starved in a superblock. What happens when the same aesthetic, backed by the same authority, facing the same prostrate society, is applied not to where people live but to how they eat, to the fields and herds that feed a country, by planners who have never farmed and are certain that farming is a science? Scott has two answers, one Soviet and one Tanzanian, and they are the darkest material this shelf has handled. He also has a word for what the planners destroyed, and a chapter arguing that the word names the kind of knowledge a society can least afford to lose. And then the critics arrive, some of whom think Scott has written the book he denied writing, and one of whom, an economist, suggests that the book's real hero is a man Scott never mentions, Friedrich Hayek. That is part two.

Next time, Seeing Like a State, part two: collectivisation, villagisation, mētis, and the case against. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Bullshit Jobs (Graeber): five types, and the two surveys that disagree
item.description: David Graeber's 2018 book on paid work that even the worker cannot justify – the five types, managerial feudalism, the polls that launched it, and the two surveys that later disagreed about whether any of it is real.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Computer That Moved Four Hundred Kilometres

One of the testimonies in the book comes from a man who worked for a subcontractor to the German military, and I want to tell it at its own pace because the whole argument is folded inside it. A soldier in a barracks wants to move a computer from one office to the office next door, a distance of about five metres. He cannot simply carry it. The army has outsourced its logistics to a private firm; that firm has passed the IT portion to a second one, and the second has handed the actual moving of equipment to a third. So the soldier fills in a form. The form goes to the first firm, which forwards it to the second, which forwards it to the third, and the third dispatches the man telling the story, who drives several hundred kilometres to the barracks, signs a document, unplugs the computer, carries it into the next room, plugs it in, signs another document, and drives home. The book's narrator does not need to add a moral; the day's mileage is the moral. Somewhere in that chain a number of people were paid, a contract was honoured, a compliance requirement was met, and a computer travelled five metres by way of a motorway.

Now ask the clinician's question about that story, the question this episode is going to keep asking: what is the denominator? The moving of the computer is a case. How many cases like it are there, out of how many working days in the German economy, and is the man telling it typical of anything or is he a memorable outlier who wrote to an anthropologist because anthropologists were asking? The book you are about to hear described is built almost entirely out of stories like this one, hundreds of them, collected from people who volunteered them. It is the most read book this shelf has covered and the least measured, and the interesting part is that the measuring was done afterwards, twice, by people who disagreed with each other about what it showed.

The question the book is about predates it by a long way, and this series has been circling it since the Parkinson episode. An organization is supposed to be a machine for turning effort into some output somebody wants. Parkinson found the effort multiplying regardless of the output; Peter found it settling into positions where it could no longer produce; the Davies episodes found the output nobody wanted being produced with enormous care because a process demanded it. What none of those books asked, because their authors were all looking at a single institution at a time, is the aggregate version. Add it all up across a whole economy, every Colonial Office clerk and every final-placement supervisor and every duplicate reporting line, and how much of the paid work in a rich country is, on the honest account of the person doing it, for nothing? Graeber's answer is a number, and the number is the problem.

Chapter Two: An Essay, a Poll, and a Book

David Graeber was introduced two episodes ago, and the biography that matters here is the same: London School of Economics, Debt: The First Five Thousand Years, the planning meetings of Occupy Wall Street, and a mother's paperwork. What comes between The Utopia of Rules and this book is an essay, and the essay's reception is half the story.

In the summer of two thousand and thirteen a small radical magazine called Strike! asked Graeber for something provocative and he gave them three thousand words titled On the Phenomenon of Bullshit Jobs. The premise was a question he attributed to Keynes: in nineteen thirty, Keynes had predicted that by the end of the century technology would have advanced enough that countries like Britain or the United States would be working a fifteen-hour week. The technology arrived. The short week did not. Graeber's essay proposed that the missing hours had not been absorbed by more production of things people want, but by the invention of work, whole categories of employment that exist without producing anything, and that the people inside those categories know it. His phrase for the damage was that it is a scar across our collective soul. The essay's most quoted move was a thought experiment: imagine a class of workers vanishing overnight and ask whether anyone would miss them. Nurses, refuse collectors, mechanics, teachers, dock workers gone, and the world is in trouble within days. Private equity executives, lobbyists, public relations researchers, actuaries, telemarketers, bailiffs, legal consultants gone, and it is not obvious how anyone would suffer. From which he drew a general rule, that the more obviously a job benefits other people, the less it tends to pay.

The essay went around the world. The magazine's website fell over under the traffic; the piece was translated into more than a dozen languages within weeks. And then the poll. In two thousand and fifteen the polling firm YouGov asked British workers whether their job made a meaningful contribution to the world. Thirty-seven percent said no, and a further thirteen percent were not sure. A Dutch survey around the same time produced a figure near forty percent. Graeber had written a provocation with a made-up range in it, somewhere between twenty and fifty percent of all jobs, and now a real poll had landed inside the range, and the provocation had become a finding, or something that could be presented as one. He asked people who felt they had bullshit jobs to write to him, several hundred did, and the book that came out in two thousand and eighteen, Bullshit Jobs: A Theory, is built on those testimonies, the poll, and a theory of why a market economy would produce this at all.

The definition, in the book, is tighter than the essay's and it is worth getting exactly right because most of the later argument turns on what it includes. A bullshit job is paid employment so pointless, unnecessary, or pernicious that even the person doing it cannot justify its existence, though the terms of employment oblige them to pretend otherwise. Two clauses carry it. The first is even the employee: this is not an outsider's judgement that your job is worthless, it is your own. The second is the obligation to pretend, which is what distinguishes a bullshit job from a merely bad one. A bad job, in Graeber's vocabulary, is one that is useful and awful: cleaning, care work, the kind of thing that would be missed within a day and is paid as though it would not. A bullshit job is one that is comfortable and hollow, and the hollowness has to be concealed, from the boss, from the family, sometimes from the worker's own account of the week.

Chapter Three: Five Ways to Be Paid for Nothing

The book's taxonomy is the part people remember, and it earns the memory, because each of the five types names a mechanism rather than a job title. Graeber is careful about that: no occupation is bullshit as such; the types describe what a role is for within an organization, whatever it is called on the door.

Flunkies exist to make somebody else feel or look important. The receptionist in an office that gets three calls a day is not there for the calls. She is there because a firm of that kind has a receptionist, and a partner who walks past an empty desk in the morning is a partner at a lesser firm. Graeber's own examples run from doormen to the assistants of assistants, and the mechanism is feudal in a way he will make explicit later: retainers whose function is the standing of the person they are attached to.

Goons exist because the other side has goons. Lobbyists, corporate lawyers, telemarketers, the publicist whose job is to counter a competitor's publicist. Graeber's test is that the role only makes sense in an adversarial frame: if every firm's lobbyists vanished at once, no firm would be worse off relative to any other, which means the aggregate contribution of the category is zero by construction. Note that the goon's job is often not pointless from the employer's point of view, which is why this type sits awkwardly in a definition built on the worker's own judgement; a good deal of the book's later trouble with critics lives in this category.

Duct tapers exist to fix a problem that should not exist. The programmer who spends his life patching code that was written badly because the firm would not pay for it to be written well; the airline employee whose entire role is calming passengers whose luggage the airline has lost, when the money spent calming them would have paid for not losing the luggage. This one connects straight back to Davies, three episodes and a companion piece into the series: the duct taper is an accountability sink with a salary, a person whose presence lets an organization keep a fault permanent by making its consequences absorbable.

Box tickers exist so that an organization can claim to be doing something it is not doing. The officer whose reports on a hospital's patient-consultation process are produced, filed, and never read, so that the hospital can say consultation occurs. The whole audit society Davies described is staffed by box tickers, and the sharp thing in Graeber's account is the worker's experience of it: box tickers frequently know the box is the product, and their job is to keep producing it convincingly.

And taskmasters exist to assign work to people who would work without being told to, or, in the second and more corrosive variant, to invent work for others, the manager who generates the checklists and the forms and the strategic-alignment exercises that the box tickers below then tick. Taskmasters of the second kind are the ones who produce bullshit jobs downstream, and Graeber's diagram of an organization in this condition is one where taskmasters at the top manufacture tasks, box tickers in the middle complete them, and duct tapers at the bottom absorb the damage, with flunkies attached to everyone senior and goons on the perimeter.

Read that structure against the shelf and it maps onto the last five books with almost no adjustment. Parkinson's officials who make work for each other are taskmasters and box tickers in a closed loop. Peter's final-placement supervisor, the person promoted one rung past competence, is very often a taskmaster of the first kind, supervising people who need no supervision because that is the only supervision he is now capable of. And Whyte's organization man, the well-adjusted middle who identified with the firm, is what a box ticker looks like before he has admitted to himself what the box is. Graeber's contribution is not that he found these people. Everyone on this shelf found them. His contribution is the claim that they are now a large fraction of the workforce, and that the fraction is not a side effect of bureaucracy but the product of a specific economic arrangement, which he names.

Chapter Four: Managerial Feudalism

Here is the puzzle the theory has to solve, and Graeber states it fairly. Under the textbook account of a market economy, bullshit jobs should not exist. A firm that pays people to do nothing is a firm with higher costs than a competitor that does not, and competition should eliminate it. That is the argument every economist made against the essay within a week of its publication, and it is a good argument. Governments might pad payrolls for political reasons, the objection goes, but private firms cannot afford to, so if the phenomenon is real it must be a public-sector phenomenon, which would be an old and unsurprising finding.

Graeber's answer is that the textbook is describing an economy we no longer have. What we have, he argues, is managerial feudalism: a system in which a growing share of the economy's surplus is captured not by producing things but by controlling flows of money, rent, and administrative position, and in which the people who capture it distribute a portion of it downward in the form of retainers, because in a system of that kind having retainers is how standing is displayed and maintained. A feudal lord does not employ a hall full of attendants because they are productive. He employs them because a lord with a small retinue is a small lord. Graeber's claim is that the managerial class in finance, in the professional services that orbit finance, in the administrative layers of universities and hospitals, has recreated exactly that logic, and that the growth of the administrative layer in every large organization since the nineteen seventies is what feudal retinues look like when they are wearing lanyards.

The mechanism has three parts, and each connects to something the shelf has already documented. The first is the one Graeber shares with the flying-cars essay two episodes ago: the redirection of the economy's investment from making things toward administering, monitoring, and financialising the things that already exist. If the profitable activity is control rather than production, then the labour that control requires, compliance, reporting, reconciliation, the manufacturing and completion of forms, grows regardless of whether anything is being made. The second part is political, and it is where Graeber is most a moralist: a population kept busy is a population that does not have the time to ask what the arrangement is for, and he suggests, without quite claiming it as a design, that the ruling class of any period has understood that a leisured, unemployed, healthy population is a danger. The third part is cultural, and it is the one his critics find hardest to dismiss. Work has become, in the rich countries, the primary source of moral standing, so that a person who does not work is a person without a claim on the respect of others, regardless of what the work produces. The result is that everybody, including the worker in a bullshit job, has a stake in the job continuing, because the alternative is not leisure but disgrace.

That third part is Whyte's Social Ethic, seventy years on and stripped of its optimism. Whyte's organization man believed that belonging to the group was a moral good in itself. Graeber's box ticker believes, or has been made to believe, the same thing about having a job, and the two beliefs are one belief with the group replaced by the payroll. What Whyte saw as the birth of a new ethic Graeber sees at the end of its life, when the belief has outlived the conditions that made it plausible, the productive firm with a real product and a real career inside it, and continues to run on its own momentum. The organization man at least had an organization. The bullshit worker has a badge that opens a door to a desk at which nothing happens.

And I would push the shelf's own frame one step further than Graeber does, because the series has an instrument he lacked. He explains why an economy would pay for hollow work. He does not quite explain why nobody inside the organization stops it, given that many of them know. The Davies series answered that: nobody in a position to stop it is running the organization. Command left the owners and did not arrive at the managers; it dissolved into the procedures between them. A taskmaster who realised tomorrow that his department produced nothing could not abolish it, because the department is now an input to three other departments' reports, and a report that arrives without its input is a compliance failure with a name attached. Bullshit jobs persist for the same reason the sinks persist: the machine that would have to catch them is the machine they are part of.

Chapter Five: The Book at Its Strongest

Before the numbers, the steelman, because the book's best chapter is not the theory. It is the chapter on what the condition does to the people in it, and here the testimonies stop being anecdotes and start being clinical material.

Graeber's expectation, and the reader's, is that a job where nothing is required of you would be experienced as a kind of freedom. Eight paid hours, no output, an internet connection. The testimonies say otherwise, consistently and in detail. The people writing to him describe anxiety, depression, a corrosion of self-respect that they cannot explain to friends who work real jobs and cannot mention to the employer who has, after all, done nothing wrong. Several describe the specific torment of having to look busy, of maintaining a performance of work for a manager who may or may not know it is a performance. One of the book's most-quoted contributors, a man whose entire job was to be present in case a rarely used system failed, describes the experience as being paid to be a piece of furniture. Graeber reaches for a concept from developmental psychology to explain the damage: the pleasure of being the cause, the infant's discovery that its actions produce effects in the world, which he argues is the root of the human sense of self. A job in which nothing you do produces any effect is not rest. It is a slow attack on the faculty that makes you a person.

That is a real observation, and it is the part of the book that the later surveys confirmed without controversy. Whatever the prevalence of the condition, the people who report it are measurably worse off. I will come back to how much worse. But the steelman is that Graeber identified a form of harm that the discipline of work had not been looking for, because its instruments measured hours, pay, safety, and satisfaction, and this harm survives all four being fine. You can be well paid, safe, working reasonable hours, reporting satisfaction on the annual survey because the survey does not have a box for this, and still be coming apart in a way that only the plain question, would anyone miss your job if it vanished, can reach. The book made that question askable. That is not nothing, and it may be most of what the book will be remembered for.

Chapter Six: The Two Surveys

Now the measuring, which is where this shelf's home lens is needed, and the finding is that the answer depends entirely on which question was asked.

The first serious test came from a Cambridge and Birmingham group, Magdalena Soffia, Alex Wood and Brendan Burchell, published in Work, Employment and Society in twenty twenty-two under the title Alienation Is Not Bullshit. They went to the European Working Conditions Survey, which asks a very large sample of workers across the European Union, every five years, a battery of questions about their jobs, one of which is how often they have the feeling of doing useful work. Take the people who answer rarely or never as the bullshit-job population and the numbers come out like this. In two thousand and five, seven point eight percent. In twenty ten, five point five. In twenty fifteen, four point eight. Not twenty to fifty percent; under five, and falling. The regional pattern was the reverse of Graeber's expectation too: the Nordic countries lowest at three percent, the British Isles and the Mediterranean highest at about five and a half. And the occupations at the top of the uselessness table were not the lobbyists and the compliance officers. They were labourers in mining, construction and transport, at fifteen percent; refuse workers, near ten; cleaners, at eight. The refuse collectors, the very people Graeber's thought experiment held up as the workers society could not do without, were among the most likely to say their own work was useless. Teachers, doctors and lawyers were at the bottom, around one percent. Graduates reported the condition at half the rate of non-graduates. The group's conclusion was that Graeber's account could not be sustained: the perception of useless work was real and was strongly associated with poor wellbeing, but it tracked bad management, lack of autonomy and disrespect rather than occupation, so that what it tracked was what Marx called alienation, a much older idea, and one that does not require a theory of managerial feudalism to explain.

The second test came a year later from Simon Walo at Zurich, in the same journal, and it reached the opposite headline. Walo used the American Working Conditions Survey from twenty fifteen, about eighteen hundred workers, and a different question: whether the respondent's job was, in their own view, socially useless, or gave them the feeling of making a positive impact on their community and society. Nineteen percent said their job was useless. And when he sorted by occupation, Graeber's categories showed up. Sales workers were two and a half times as likely as everyone else to consider their jobs useless; business and finance roughly twice; managers nearly twice; office and administrative support about one and three-quarter times. Legal work leaned the same way but did not reach significance. Those ratios survived adjustment for the very factors Soffia's group had said explained everything, the routine content of the work, the autonomy, the quality of management. Walo's verdict was that Graeber's theory had robust support, at least in what he called the heavily financialised Anglo-Saxon economies, while also finding that the alienation variables mattered too, so that useless work was multifactorial rather than any one thing.

So one study says five percent and falling and the wrong occupations, and the other says nineteen percent and the right ones. Both are competent. Both are in the same journal. How does a listener decide?

This is the moment the shelf's own instruments earn their keep, because the disagreement is not really about bullshit jobs. It is about a question this series has met twice already in other clothes: the rate you get depends on what you count, and the same statistic differs when the frame differs. Look at the two questions. The European survey asks how often you feel you are doing useful work. That is a question about the experience of the working day; a refuse collector on a bad crew under a contemptuous supervisor, doing objectively vital work, can answer never, and he is not wrong about his week. The American survey asks whether the job is socially useless or makes a positive impact on society. That is a question about the job's standing in the world, and a sales executive who is well managed and autonomous can answer useless, and he is not wrong about the job. Graeber's definition was the second kind of question: the worker's judgement of the job's contribution, not the worker's feeling of usefulness on a Tuesday. Soffia's group measured alienation and found alienation. Walo measured the thing Graeber described and found something like it, at a rate about half of the YouGov figure that started the whole affair, and concentrated where the book said it would be.

Which means the honest reading is narrower than either headline. The book's number, twenty to fifty percent, does not survive. Its map, that the condition concentrates in finance, sales, administration and management rather than in the useful-and-awful jobs, does survive, at least in the United States, at around one worker in five, and about one in nine in the occupations the book did not accuse. And the mechanism that best explains the remainder of the variation is not feudalism but the old and boring one, the quality of the relationship between a worker and the people above him. Graeber is right about where the hollow jobs are and wrong about how many there are, and the thing he most wanted to be right about, that the hollowness is a structural product of financialised capitalism rather than of bad bosses, is the part the evidence splits on, with the better-designed test of his own definition leaning his way.

Chapter Seven: The Case Against

The critics had assembled before either survey and their counts should be heard at full strength, because the strongest of them are about the book's method rather than its number.

Michael Robbins, reviewing it for The Nation, put the central objection in one sentence: the book's reliance on workers' subjective impressions of whether their work has value is its major weakness. A testimony is a self-selected story told to a sympathetic collector. The several hundred people who wrote to Graeber were people who had read an essay about bullshit jobs, recognised themselves in it, and wanted to be in the book. No one who read the essay and thought, that is not me, wrote in to say so. The book's evidence base is a case series with no controls. A series like that can establish that a condition exists and describe what it looks like, which Graeber did well, but it cannot say how common the condition is, and the book's central claim is about prevalence. Robbins also caught a factual problem the Bureau of Labor Statistics could have fixed for free: the fastest-growing job categories in the United States are not information and administrative work but care work and food service, useful-and-awful jobs, the opposite of what the theory predicts is expanding.

The second count is the feudalism. Robbins again, and he is not alone: an economy in which surplus is extracted from the labour of others by the owners of capital is a capitalist economy, whatever its retinues look like, and calling it feudal does not make the profit motive disappear from the firms that employ flunkies. The word does rhetorical work; it does not do analytical work. The taskmaster who hires a retinue is still, on the shelf's account, a component of a machine optimising for something, and the interesting question, which the book never quite reaches, is what that something is. Davies's answer, that the machine is optimising for the survival of its own procedures, explains the retinue without needing the lord.

The third count is about the taxonomy, and Andrew Anthony in The Observer made it briskly: the five types are arbitrary distinctions dressed as discoveries. A goon's job is not bullshit to the firm that pays for it; a duct taper is doing real work on a real problem; a flunky in a service economy is delivering a service, standing, that the customer demonstrably wants.
